rules.statement: In the English sentence This is good, IS is part of the verb to be. In Gupapuyŋu this type of sentence has no such verb. It is a verbless sentence.
Words like good, bad, little, big are adjectives. They describe what something is like.
Order of words in a sentence is not necessarily fixed. It is quite correct to say Manymak dhuwala, especially if manymak is being emphasised.

lessons.title: Introducing nouns

rules.statement: Nouns (in this case) are things which can be seen and handled.
Dhuwali + noun = That is a X.
Noun + adjective = The X is Y, verbless.
Dhuwala/Dhuwali + noun + adjective = This/That X is Y, which can also read This is a Y X.
Nhä dhuwala? = What is this? Nhä dhuwali? = What is that?

notes: The English of sections 3 and 4 can also read: This is a short spear, That is new grass, etc
The book prints Dhuwall gurtha, typo for Dhuwali

rules.statement: In Gupapuyŋu, verbs fall into nine different groups, and each verb has 4 different forms, called Primary, Secondary, Tertiary and Quaternary.
When the secondary form of the verb is used by itself, it is a command.
Group 1: all forms remain unchanged throughout.
Group 2: primary form ends in -i, remains unchanged for secondary.
Group 3: primary form ends in -a, changed to -i in the secondary.
To make commands negative, use yaka before the secondary form.

lessons.title: More commands

rules.statement: Group 4: primary form ends in -irri, which changes to -i for the secondary.
Group 5: primary form ends in -un, which changes to -urru for secondary.
Group 6: primary form ends in -an, which changes to -ulu for secondary.
In some examples it (or him or her) is needed in English to make sense. In Gupapuyŋu the verb is often used by itself, it (etc) being understood.

notes: Nherrpulu printed for put it, the word lists give nhirrpan Vtr-II nhirrpulu and nherran Vtr-III nherrara — user confirmed: Nherrpulu = put it, as printed
Ask: reverse list p22 prints ŋäŋ'thun but verb table p47 and wordlist p58 print ŋäṉ'thun, aligned to ŋäṉ'thun (book-internal split confirmed by user; engine keeps ŋäṉ')

lessons.title: Introducing personal pronouns

rules.statement: In English a personal pronoun is either singular or plural. In Gupapuyŋu it is singular (one person), dual (two people) or plural (more than two).
In Gupapuyŋu there is an inclusive as well as an exclusive form of WE. Inclusive means person addressed is included. Exclusive means person addressed is excluded.
Ŋilimurru and ŋilinyu are sometimes pronounced ŋalimurru and ŋalinyu.
The prefix ŋi- (or ŋa-) is often dropped from ŋanapurru, ŋilinyu and ŋarra. In Yirrkala dialects and some at Elcho, the prefix is always retained.

examples.en: We two are good (s/he & I, not you)
We are good (you & we/you pl & I)
We (3 or more - not you) are good
We are sinful (inclusive, sermon: speaker, missionaries and Aboriginal folk all included)
We are sinful (exclusive, prayer: person addressed excluded)

notes: Sermon example: inclusive must be used or the yolŋu would be excluded
The book illustrates inclusive vs exclusive with an address example: the exclusive excludes the person addressed from the group described (religious example omitted by request)

lessons.title: More commands

rules.statement: Group 7: primary form ends in -ma (not -gama or -kama) which changes to -ŋu for secondary.
Group 8: primary form ends in -gama or -kama, which changes to -guŋu or -kuŋu for secondary.
Some irregular verbs: Ganarrthulu! Ŋayathulu! Ŋäku! Buŋu!
The form mänŋu is often used instead of märraŋu in Gupapuyŋu. Both words mean the same.

Gäma (take/bring/carry) and märrama (take/get) are apt to be confused. The act of receiving is märrama; taking or carrying it along is gäma. The yolŋu get (märrama) their food at the store then take (gäma) it to the camp. The man will take (märrama) a wife; the man will take (gäma) his wife to the camp.
At Yirrkala, gäma (not gurrukama) is used for wear.

notes: Although the word it is needed in English to make sense, it is usually omitted in Gupapuyŋu
Ḻawuŋu printed without ä, the word list gives ḻäwuma Vtr-II ḻäwuŋu

lessons.title: Future tense (1): tomorrow future

rules.statement: There are various types of future tense. The TOMORROW FUTURE is used for any event in the future, from tomorrow onwards, when a definite time is stated or inferred (next week, next month, next year). It is formed with the particle dhu plus the SECONDARY form of the verb.
Negative: dhu yaka + verb. Goḏarr' ŋarra dhu yaka buḻ'yurru = I shall not play tomorrow.
Dhu is merely a verb particle, receives no emphasis, tacked on to the preceding word, sounds like thu but spelt dhu (Spelling Rule 5, Alphabet Lesson 23).
The particle yurru is often used instead of dhu. Both mean the same. At Yirrkala it is always yurru, never dhu.
Word order in a sentence is not fixed.

notes: Suggestions: make similar sentences by revising verbs in Lessons 3, 4 and 6, and substituting other personal pronouns for ŋarra

lessons.title: Derived words (1): noun plus -mirri = adjective

rules.statement: The suffix -mirri is added to a noun to form an adjective meaning having or possessing that noun, like English -ful. Yothumirri = having or possessing a child, with child (pregnant). In many cases no English word exists equivalent to them, so a group of words is used to translate.

examples.en: This tin has food in it
This tin has water in it
This tin has a string on it
This book has songs in it
This book has stories in it
This place is full of rubbish

notes: The above words ending in -mirri are called adjectives, because they tell us something about the noun

rules.statement: The suffix -miriw is the opposite of -mirri. Added to a noun it forms an adjective indicating not possessing, without, like English -less. Yothumiriw = without a child, childless.
-miriw without has a retroflexed r, -mirri with has a rolled r. See Alphabet and Pronunciation Lesson 30.
The present continuous tense (the action is happening now and continuing) is formed by using ga with the PRIMARY form of the verb.
Ga is merely a verb particle, receives no emphasis, tacked on to the preceding word, often sounds like ka but spelt ga (Spelling Rule 5, Lesson 18).
Word order is not fixed: Ŋarra djäma ga and Djäma ŋarra ga are both correct. Often the word to be emphasised is placed first.
Yirrkala dialects use yukurra instead of ga to indicate present continuous.

lessons.title: Future tense 2: same-day future

rules.statement: The SAME-DAY FUTURE is used for any verb which will be performed today. It is formed with the particle dhu plus the PRIMARY form of the verb.

A verb in the INDEFINITE future (no definite time stipulated or inferred) is usually put into the same-day future. Ŋarra dhu roŋiyirri = I shall return. This also applies to events in the far distant future where no definite time is stated.
Negative: dhu yaka + primary form. Ŋarra dhu yaka roŋiyirri = I won't return.
Nhaltjan nhe dhu? = What will you do?

notes: Notes 1, 2, 3 of Lesson 7 apply also to these examples

rules.statement: An adverb of PLACE tells us WHERE an action occurs. Djinaga ŋayi ga nhina = He is sitting inside.
These place adverbs are stationary. They cannot be used in this form with verbs denoting movement (go, run etc).
An adverb of TIME tells us WHEN an action occurs. Ŋarra yurru marrtji goḏarr' = I'll go tomorrow.

In many cases a word is both an adjective and an adverb. Modifying a noun or pronoun it is an adjective, modifying a verb it is an adverb: bulu ŋatha = more food, bulu marrtji = go again, maṉḏa rrambaŋi = they are equal, maṉḏa ga rrambaŋi nhina = they are sitting together.
The position of words in a sentence is not fixed.

lessons.title: Possessive adjectives (1a): noun plus -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu

rules.statement: When the noun ends in a vowel (a/i/u) or a vowel plus glottal stop (a'/i'/u') the possessive suffix -wa is added: Djäwawa, Bäpa'wa, yothuwa.
When the noun ends in a stop (p/t/ṯ/tj/k/') the suffix -ku is added: Ninimbitjku, miyalkku, Burralaŋ'ku.
When the noun ends in a nasal (m/n/ṉ/ny/ŋ) or a liquid (l/ḻ/r/rr) or y or w, the suffix -gu is added: Stephengu, Balimaŋgu, Mawuyulgu, Djupandawuygu.
Yolku dhuwala guya? = Whose fish is that? Yolku is an exception to the rule.

At Yirrkala -wu is used instead of -wa (Bäpawu, Djäwawu). At Yirrkala, and sometimes at Elcho and Milingimbi, the suffix -wu follows liquids, liquids plus glottal, w or y, and w'/y' (Banyguḻwu, Yälparrwu).

notes: Word order in a sentence is not fixed

lessons.title: Possessive adjectives (1b): personal pronouns

rules.statement: Possessive adjectives are formed by adding the suffix -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu to a personal pronoun, with some irregularities: ŋarraku my, nhuŋu your, nhanŋu his/her, ŋalitjalaŋgu our dual inclusive, ŋalinyalaŋgu our dual exclusive, nhumalaŋgu your, ŋalimurruŋgu our plural inclusive, ŋanapurruŋgu our plural exclusive, walalaŋgu their.
Prefix ŋi- is sometimes used instead of ŋa- when the following vowel is -i: ŋilitjalaŋgu, ŋilinyalaŋgu, ŋilimurruŋgu.
In Gupapuyŋu the prefix ŋa- (or ŋi-) is often dropped: rraku my, limurruŋgu our.
At Yirrkala ŋitjalaŋgu and ŋinyalaŋgu are the dual forms of our.
English of these sentences can also read: This fish is mine.

notes: See Lesson 5 for inclusive, exclusive and dual

lessons.title: Djäl and Marŋgi

rules.statement: Even though we translate djäl and marŋgi by using English verbs want and know, in Gupapuyŋu they are really adjectives. The verbalised forms are djälthirri and marŋgithirri.

The English equivalent of djäl would be something like in want (of)/in need (of)/desirous (of). For example: Ŋarra djäl gapuwa. I (am) in want of water. Djäl always puts the suffix -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu on the thing or person desired.

The English equivalent of marŋgi would be something like aware (of)/informed/knowledgeable. For example: Ŋarra marŋgi. I am informed. ie. I know. Marŋgi always puts the suffix -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu on the thing or person known.
Marŋgi is also used in the sense: know all about/have had experience with/be familiar with. Ŋarra marŋgi yarraman'ku = I know all about horses.
Negative: Yaka ŋarra nhuŋu djäl = I don't want you. Ŋarra yaka nhanŋu marŋgi = I don't know him.
Nhaku nhe djäl? = What do you (one person) want?
Yolku nhe djäl? = Whom do you want?

examples.en: I want some meat/a bird/an animal
I know all about horses/I have had experience with horses
I know all about guns/I can use a gun/I have had experience with guns
I am familiar with yams/I have tasted yams

notes: To determine which form of the suffix -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu is added to a Noun, see Rules in Lesson 13
Notes 1 and 2 of Lesson 13 re varying pronunciations at Yirrkala etc also apply to this Lesson
Don't worry that a Gupapuyŋu adjective in this Lesson has been translated by an English verb. No language can be translated into another using exact equivalents
In Lessons 13 and 14 the suffix -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu was added to Nouns and Personal Pronouns and the products were called Possessive Adjectives (Balimaŋgu = Balimaŋ's, ŋarraku = my)
Word order in sentence is not fixed
Some native speakers do not put a glottal stop in: djamarrkuḻiwa, Djulibiŋgu, Mawalangu (Lesson 13), warrakangu, gulakawa (Lesson 15)
Reverse list p25 prints warrakan without glottal, lesson prints warrakan'ku: both attested, see note 6

lessons.title: Past tense (1): same-day past

rules.statement: There are various types of past tense in Gupapuyŋu. One of these we shall call the SAME-DAY-PAST. This form is used for any event which has already happened TODAY. To form the SAME-DAY-PAST the TERTIARY form of the verb is used.
Group 1 verbs usually have particle gana, to be dealt with in Lesson 18.
Group 2: primary form ends in -i. Add -na to form tertiary.
Group 3: primary form ends in -a. Add -na to form tertiary.
Group 4: primary form ends in -rri. Tertiary changes -rri to -na.
Group 5: primary form ends in -un. Tertiary changes -un to -urruna.
Group 6: primary form ends in -an, which changes to -ara for Tertiary.
Group 7: primary form ends in -ma, which changes to -ŋala for Tertiary.
Group 8: primary form ends in -gama/-kama which changes to -gaŋala/-kaŋala for Tertiary.
Irregular: Ŋäkula (heard), bumara (hit), ganarrthaŋala (left), ŋayathaŋala (held).
The SAME-DAY-PAST form is also often used for any action in the indefinite past where no actual time is either stated or inferred, even though the incident may have occurred a long while ago.

notes: Be sure you are emphasising FIRST syllable only
Word order in a sentence is not fixed
The Mawalan example dhiŋgama (die) is introduced in this lesson

lessons.title: Past tense (2): yesterday past

rules.statement: Another type of past tense is one we shall call the YESTERDAY-PAST tense. This form is used for any event which took place YESTERDAY or at any time in the recent past (apart from today) especially when a definite time is stated or inferred (for example: last week/last month etc). To form the YESTERDAY-PAST tense, the PRIMARY form of the verb is used.

notes: Word order is not fixed
Barpuru = yesterday, introduced in this lesson

lessons.title: Continuous aspect of verb

rules.statement: The Continuous Form is indicated by three particles: ga with a verb in the PRIMARY form, gi with a verb in the SECONDARY form, gana with a verb in the TERTIARY form.
Yesterday-past continuous (cf Lesson 17): Barpuru ŋarra ga djäma = I was working yesterday.
Same-day-future continuous (cf Lesson 11): Maṉḏa dhu ga weyin nhina = They will be staying for a long time.
Tomorrow-future continuous (cf Lesson 7): Goḏarr' ŋarra dhu gi buḻ'yurru = Tomorrow I shall be playing. Particle used with Quaternary Form will be introduced later.
Continuous commands (cf Lessons 3, 4): Dhärri gi! = Stand!/Stay standing! Djäka (or djäga) gi! = Look after (it)! Negative: Yaka nhe gi waŋi! = Don't (you) talk!
Same-day-past continuous (cf Lesson 16): Ŋayi gana ŋäthina = He was crying. Ŋayi gana djäma = He was working.

The continuous aspect is far more common in Gupapuyŋu than in English. Often in Gupapuyŋu, if the action CONTINUES over any period of time the CONTINUOUS indicator is used, whereas in English we wouldn't use it at all. For example: Ŋarra dhu ga ḻupthun, I'll have a wash.
At Yirrkala yukurra, yukurri and yukurrana are the signs of continuous aspect.

examples.en: They will be staying for a long time
They will be waiting for a long time

notes: English translations could just as well be: I worked yesterday, They will stay for a long time, Tomorrow I'll listen etc
ga, gi and gana receive no emphasis, tacked on to the preceding word, sound like ka, ki, kana (Spelling Rule 5)
Word order in a sentence is not fixed
buthuru-bitjun (listen, Gp-5) and the djäga variant of djäka appear in this lesson

lessons.title: Object of a verb (1): suffix -nha added to person

rules.statement: In Gupapuyŋu word order is not fixed. The suffix -nha is added to the Object of the verb, when that object is a person.

notes: Word order is not fixed
Gäthura = today and yapa = sister are introduced in this lesson

lessons.title: Object of a verb (2): suffix -nha added to personal pronoun

rules.statement: Personal pronouns often occur as the Object of a Verb. In such cases -nha is added to the forms listed in Lesson 5, although in some cases there are irregularities: ŋarranha me, nhuna you, ŋanya her/him, ŋalitjalanha us (you and me), ŋalinyalanha us, nhumalanha you, maṉḏanha them (2), ŋalimurrunha us, ŋanapurrunha us, walalanha them.

notes: See Lesson 5 re inclusive, exclusive, dual etc
Prefix ŋi- is sometimes used instead of ŋa- when preceding i: ŋilinyalanha, ŋilimurrunha
In Gupapuyŋu prefix ŋa- (or ŋi-) is often dropped: limurrunha
At Yirrkala ŋitjalanha and ŋinyalanha are the dual forms of our
Word order is not fixed

lessons.title: Object of a verb (3): no suffix added to thing

rules.statement: In Gupapuyŋu, when the Object of a verb is a THING (not a person) quite often no suffix at all is used.

examples.en: We lost the book/forgot the book

notes: -nha is usually, though not always, omitted from these objects because there is no ambiguity without it
The suffix -na is sometimes added, but this carries an entirely different meaning from -nha. This will be dealt with in a later Lesson
Word order is not fixed

New in this lesson: guyaŋa (remember/think), wurrthun (pull out), dhuḻ'yun (build), dhuŋgur'yun (light), ŋupan (chase), ŋarali' (tobacco), bala' (house), lipalipa (canoe), bathi (dilly-bag), maypal (shellfish); ḻuka also = drink, moma also = lose, ŋayathama also = reach, buma also = gather

lessons.title: Agent (subject of transitive verb): suffix -dhu/-thu/-yu/-y

rules.statement: All verbs which have a direct object (see Lessons 19 and 20) are Transitive, whether that object is expressed or not. All verbs of Lesson 21 are Transitive Verbs. In Gupapuyŋu the Subject of a Transitive Verb will be called the AGENT. The suffix -dhu/-thu/-yu/-y is added to the Agent when the Agent is a Noun (not a Personal Pronoun).
When the Agent ends in a vowel (a/i/u) or a vowel plus glottal (a'/i'/u') the suffix -y is added: Djäway, Bäyay, Bäpay, Yuwatiy, Lorruy, Ḏirramuy.
When the Agent ends in a liquid (l/ḻ/r/rr) or a liquid plus glottal stop, or -y or -w or -y' or -w', the suffix -yu is added: Mawuyulyu, Marmburryu, Djupandawuyyu, Mäw'yu.
When the Agent ends in a nasal (m/n/ṉ/ny/ŋ) the suffix -dhu is added: Stephendhu, Balimaŋdhu, Djimbuṉdhu, Djirinydhu.
When the Agent ends in a stop (apart from glottal) ie p/t/ṯ/tj/k or a nasal plus glottal (m'/n'/ṉ'/ny'/ŋ') the suffix -thu is added: Wandjukthu, Miyalkthu, Ninimbitjthu, Ŋarrtjam'thu, Wurrpaṉ'thu.
Yolthu nhuna bumara? = Who hit you? (Yolthu is an exception to the rule.)
When the Agent is a Personal Pronoun, no suffix is added: Ŋayi ŋarranha bumara. He hit me.

notes: At Yirrkala, the suffix -yu is added instead of -y (Section E). For example: Bäpayu/ḏarramuyu
When -y is added to a word which ends in a glottal stop, it precedes the glottal (for example: djamarrkuḻiy'). Remember some speakers do not put glottal stop in djamarrkuḻi' at all
When the Agent is a Personal Pronoun, no suffix is added: Ŋayi ŋarranha bumara. He hit me
Word order in a sentence is not fixed

lessons.title: Transitive verbs

rules.statement: Some words in Gupapuyŋu are Transitive and they always behave as Transitive Verbs whether an Object is expressed or not. The suffix dealt with in Lesson 22 is added to the Agent even with no expressed Object.
Questions and answers: Yolthu ḻakaraŋala? Who told? Answer: Djäway. Djäwa did. The answer is the agent-suffixed noun alone (or the bare pronoun: Ŋarra, I did).

notes: Most verbs which are transitive in English are transitive also in Gupapuyŋu, although there are a few exceptions

djaw'yun (take away) is introduced in this lesson

lessons.title: Intransitive verbs

rules.statement: An Intransitive Verb is one which has no Object. The doer of an Intransitive Verb is called the SUBJECT (the doer of a Transitive Verb is called the AGENT). No suffix is added to the Subject of an Intransitive Verb.
Yol marrtjina? Who went? (yol without suffix for intransitive verbs; answers are bare: Djäwa, Mäw', Ŋarra).

Marrtji usually means go. However, when modified by another word, it can mean come: Marrtji räli (Lesson 27D) walk towards speaker = come; Ŋayi marrtjina räli, He came; Marrtji go! Come. When arrive can be substituted for come, buna is the best word to use: P buna, S buni, T bunana, Q bunanha(ra). Yol bunana? Who came/arrived? Bäpa yurru buna, Bäpa will come/arrive; Bäpa yurru marrtji, Bäpa will go.

notes: Most verbs which are intransitive in English are intransitive in Gupapuyŋu also, although there are a few exceptions
gitkitthun (laugh) and buna (arrive) are introduced in this lesson; räli (towards speaker) is deferred to Lesson 27D
The answer names printed are Gumuk (L23) and Gunmuk (L24) — proper names, confirmed as printed

lessons.title: Adverbial expression (1): place, thing plus -ŋura

rules.statement: Adverbial Expressions of Place are derived from nouns by addition of the suffix -ŋura: wäŋaŋura in the camp, ḏiltjiŋura in the bush, gapuŋura in the water, mulmuŋura on the grass, mitjiyaŋŋura on the boat, dhukarrŋura on the path, dhakalŋura on the island, dhawaḏaŋura on the beach, schoolŋura at school. -ŋura is added to things only, not to people.

Some pure adverbs of place of Lesson 12 can be used with derived adverbial expressions: djinaga bala'ŋura inside the hut, galki gurthaŋura near the fire. In such instances the suffix -ŋura must be added to the noun. It is wrong to say djinaga bala'.

The verb to be, when used with adverbial expressions of place, is usually translated by verbs: nhina/sit, dhärra/stand, ŋorra/lie, gorruma/be up in, up on. These cannot be used indiscriminately: nhina ga for people; ŋorra ga for things in a lying position (string on a rock); dhärra ga for things which are standing (tin on table). The yolŋu think of boats and canoes as standing: Mitjiyaŋ dhärra ga gapuŋura, the boat is in the water.
It is not necessary to add -ŋura to the name of a place: Galiwin'ku ŋayi ga nhina, He is at Elcho.
Wanha Djäwa? Where is Djäwa? Answers: Barrku (far away), Ḏiltjiŋura (in the bush), Galki gunḏaŋura (near the rock), Galiwin'ku (at Elcho).

examples.en: They are playing in the camp
They are playing in the bush
They are playing in the water
They are playing on the grass
They are playing on the boat
They are playing on the path/road
They are playing on the island
They are playing on the beach
They are playing inside the hut
They are playing near the fire
The string is on the rock
The tin is on the table
The child is in the tree

notes: -ŋura is added to things only, not to people
Be careful to pronounce ŋ as ng in sing, and tongue should be turned back for r
Word order in a sentence is not fixed
The C example reads galki gurthaŋura (user re-checked: no glottal on the page)
New in this lesson: ḏiltji, mitjiyaŋ, dhukarr, dhakal, dhawaḏa, gunḏa, and the loans school and table; gorruma (be up in/on) is the fourth posture verb

lessons.title: Adverbial expression (1): place, person plus -gala/-kala/-wala

rules.statement: To form an adverbial expression of Place, -ŋura is added to a THING but the suffix -gala/-kala/-wala is added to a PERSON. Vowel or vowel plus glottal → -wala (Djäwawala, djamarrkuḻi'wala, yothuwala). Nasal (m/n/ṉ/ny/ŋ) → -gala (Burrminygala, Raymangala, Djimbuṉgala). Stop (p/t/ṯ/tj/k) or nasal plus glottal → -kala (Miyalkkala, Wandjukkala, Yawirriny'kala, Gämuruŋ'kala). Liquid or y/w → -gala or -wala (Garmburrgala/Garmburrwala). Liquid plus glottal or y'/w' → -kala or -wala (Mäw'kala/Mäw'wala).

The suffix -gala/-kala/-wala is also added to the Personal Pronouns: ŋarrakala with me, nhokala with you, nhanukala with her/him, ŋalitjalaŋgala, ŋalinyalaŋgala, nhumalaŋgala, maṉḏaŋgala, ŋalimurruŋgala, ŋanapurruŋgala, walalaŋgala.
Some pure adverbs of place (Lesson 12) can also be used with these derived adverbial expressions: Nhini galki ŋarrakala, Sit near me.
Yolkala ŋayi ga nhina? Whom is he with? Answer: Wandjukkala.

examples.en: He is sitting with the women
He is sitting with the single boys

notes: At Yirrkala -wala is always used after a liquid or liquid plus glottal or y/y'/w/w'
Prefix ŋi- is sometimes used instead of ŋa- when following vowel is i: ŋilimurruŋgala. Prefix often dropped: limurruŋgala. At Yirrkala ŋitjalaŋgala and ŋinyalaŋgala are the dual forms of with us
Word order in a sentence is not fixed
L22 printed the name as Djimbuṉ, this lesson prints Djimbuṉgala (Djimbuṉ, consistent with L22 — user re-checked)
yawirriny' (single boys) is introduced in this lesson

lessons.title: Adverbial expression (2): movement towards, thing or place plus -lili, person plus -gala/-kala/-wala

rules.statement: When there is movement TOWARDS a thing or place, the suffix -lili is added: wäŋalili, storelili, ḏiltjilili, dhakallili, gapulili, dhawaḏalili, schoollili, Darwinlili, tablelili, bala'lili, mitjiyaŋlili, dharpalili, molulili, gurthalili.
The suffix -lili can also be added to pure adverbs of place (Lesson 12) to denote movement towards: djinaga'lili, warraŋullili, garrwarlili, barrkulili, galkilili.
The suffix -gala/-kala/-wala added to a person is equivalent to -lili added to a thing or place. It is the same suffix as that used to denote stationary position (Lesson 26).

Two very common adverbs of movement are bala (movement away from speaker) and räli (movement towards speaker): Gäŋu bala storelili (Take it to the store), Gäŋu räli storelili (Bring it to the store), Marrtji bala wäŋalili (Go to the camp), Marrtji räli wäŋalili (Come to the camp), Yänguŋu räli ŋarrakala (Send it to me), Nhäŋu bala (Look that way), Nhäŋu räli (Look this way).
Nhäkurru nhe ga marrtji? Where are you (one person) going? or Nhäkurru? Where to? Answers are allative fragments: Wäŋalili, Bala wäŋalili, Ṉathalili, Gurthalili, Guyalili.
Yolkala nhe gurrupara? To whom did you give it? Answer: Yapawala.

lessons.title: Adverbial expression (3): movement away from, thing or place plus -ŋuru

rules.statement: When there is movement away from a thing or place, the suffix -ŋuru is added: wäŋaŋuru, ḏiltjiŋuru, dhakalŋuru, Darwinŋuru, Galiwin'kuŋuru, storeŋuru, mitjiyaŋŋuru, moluŋuru, gurthaŋuru, bala'ŋuru.

The suffix -ŋuru can also be added to pure adverbs of place (Lesson 12) to denote movement away from: djinaga'ŋuru, garrwarŋuru, barrkuŋuru. Both members of a complex expression take the suffix: garrwarŋuru dharpaŋuru (from the top of the tree), barrkuŋuru wäŋaŋuru (from a country far away).
Wanhaŋuru nhe marrtjina? Where did/have you come from? Answers: Ḏiltjiŋuru (from the bush), Barrkuŋuru (from afar), Weṯiŋuru (from hunting wallabies).
Nhäŋuru ŋayi galkirrina? What/Where did he fall from? Answers: Dharpaŋuru (from a tree), Bala'ŋuru garrwarŋuru (from the top of the hut).

lessons.title: Adverbial expression (3): movement away from, person plus -galaŋuŋuru/-kalaŋuŋuru/-walaŋuŋuru

rules.statement: In Lesson 28 the suffix -ŋuru was added to things and places to denote movement away from. The same suffix (-ŋuru) is added to a person, but the infix -galaŋu/-kalaŋu/-walaŋu is inserted. See Lesson 26 for rules as to which form of the suffix is used (for example: when a person ends in a nasal m/n/ṉ/ny/ŋ the suffix -galaŋuŋuru is added): Yapawalaŋuŋuru, Djimbuṉgalaŋuŋuru, Gämuruŋ'kalaŋuŋuru, Mawuyulgalaŋuŋuru.

The suffix -galaŋuŋuru/-kalaŋuŋuru/-walaŋuŋuru is also added to the personal pronouns of Lesson 5: ŋarrakalaŋuŋuru, nhokalaŋuŋuru, nhanukalaŋuŋuru, ŋalitjalaŋgalaŋuŋuru, ŋalinyalaŋgalaŋuŋuru, nhumalaŋgalaŋuŋuru, maṉḏaŋgalaŋuŋuru, ŋalimurruŋgalaŋuŋuru, ŋanapurruŋgalaŋuŋuru, walalaŋgalaŋuŋuru.

notes: Sometimes the suffix -galaŋuŋuru/-kalaŋuŋuru/-walaŋuŋuru is abbreviated to -gala/-kala/-wala. However, when ambiguity is likely to occur the full suffix is used: Ŋayi bilyurruna ŋarrakala (He turned to me) vs Ŋayi bilyurruna ŋarrakalaŋuŋuru (He turned from me)

lessons.title: Adverbial expression (4): from, person plus -guŋu/-kuŋu/-wuŋu

rules.statement: Another suffix added to people and indicating 'from' is -guŋu/-kuŋu/-wuŋu. See Lesson 26 for rules as to which form of the suffix is used (g follows nasal, w follows vowel, etc.): Djäwawuŋu, Lorruwuŋu, Raymanguŋu, Wandjukkuŋu, Djupandawuyguŋu/-wuŋu, djamarrkuḻi'wuŋu, yawirriny'kuŋu, miyalkkuŋu.

The suffix -guŋu/-kuŋu/-wuŋu can also be added to the personal pronouns of Lesson 5: ŋarrakuŋu, nhokuŋu, nhanukuŋu, ŋalitjalaŋguŋu, ŋalinyalaŋguŋu, maṉḏaŋguŋu, ŋalimurruŋguŋu, ŋanapurruŋguŋu, nhumalaŋguŋu, walalaŋguŋu.

The difference between -guŋu/-kuŋu/-wuŋu and -galaŋuŋuru/-kalaŋuŋuru/-walaŋuŋuru: (a) if the whole body is involved in the movement, -galaŋuŋuru is used (Bilyurruna ŋayi miyalkkalaŋuŋuru); (b) if the English translation can be 'away from', -galaŋuŋuru is used (Ŋurrkuŋu barrkulili ŋarrakalaŋuŋuru, Cast it far away from me); (c) when no actual movement is implied -guŋu/-kuŋu/-wuŋu is generally used (Ŋarra dhäwu märraŋala nhanukuŋu, I got the story from him).

lessons.title: Adverbial expression (5): purpose, noun or pronoun plus -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu

rules.statement: Another use of suffix -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu is to denote purpose of an action. See Lesson 13 for rules as to which form of the suffix must be used (for example: after vowel suffix -wa is used): Ŋayi marrtjina ŋathawa (He went for food), guyawa, weṯiwa, gapuwa, gurthawa, maypalgu, buŋgulgu, miyalkku.

The suffix also marks the person an action is for: Guya ŋayi dharpuŋala Bäyawa (He speared a fish for Bäya), ŋäṉḏiwa, Marmburrgu, Wandjukku, Balimaŋgu. Yothu ga ŋäthi ŋäminiwa (The baby is crying for milk), ŋathawa, Gämuruŋ'ku, ŋäṉḏi'mirriŋuwa (for its mother).
See Lesson 14 for the personal pronouns plus suffix -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu: Maypal ŋayi bumara ŋarraku (She gathered shellfish for me), nhuŋu, nhumalaŋgu, nhanŋu, ŋilimurruŋgu, walalaŋgu.

lessons.title: More uses of -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu: (A) indirect object, (B) verb have

rules.statement: The English Indirect Object (Mary sang HIM a song — the object in front of which 'to' or 'for' can be inserted) is usually translated into Gupapuyŋu by use of the suffix -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu: Ŋarra maṉḏaŋgu bathi bumara (I made them a basket).

Another common use of suffix -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu is to indicate POSSESSION, where in English we would normally use verb 'have': Balimaŋgu miyalk ḻurrkun' (Balimaŋ has three wives), Ŋarraku djäma yindi (I have a lot of work), Ḻinyalaŋgu bäyŋu ŋatha (We have no food), Nhanŋu yapa märrma' (He has two sisters), Walalaŋgu waŋgany yäna ṉaku (They have only one canoe). This is not the only way of translating 'have'.

lessons.title: Adverbial expression (6): instrument, thing plus -dhu/-thu/-yu/-y, person plus -gala/-kala/-wala

rules.statement: The suffix -dhu/-thu/-yu/-y is added to a Thing (not a Person) to denote the INSTRUMENT by/with which an action takes place. When a person is the Instrument by which an action takes place, the suffix -gala/-kala/-wala is added: Ŋarra nhanŋu djorra' djuy'yurruna Lorruwala (I sent him a letter by/with Lorru), Laklakkala, Ŋarrtjam'kala, yawirriny'kala, Balimaŋgala; Girri' ŋayi Bäpawa djuy'yurruna ŋarrakala (He sent some things to father with/by me), maṉḏaŋgala, nhanukala, ḻinyalaŋgala.

lessons.title: Adjectives agreeing with nouns

rules.statement: In Gupapuyŋu an adjective must always possess a suffix equivalent to the suffix attached to the noun it modifies. Any adjective modifying a suffixed noun must possess the equivalent suffix, and the FORM of each suffix depends on the last sound of the ADJECTIVE itself (-wa follows vowel: yindiwa; -dhu follows nasal: weyindhu; borumgu ŋathawa).

The agreement applies across every case: dative/purpose -gu (Ŋarra djäl guyawa yindiwa; Borumgu ŋathawa walala marrtjina), object -nha (Barpuru ŋarra nhäma yuṯanha miyalknha), agent -dhu (Ḻurrkun'thu yolŋuy ŋäkula; Maḏakarritjthu bumara miyalkthu), no suffix on Vin subjects (Waŋgany yothu dhiŋgaŋala; Dharrwa yolŋu marrtjina), place -ŋura (watharrŋura bala'ŋura galki), person -gala (Miyalkkala waŋganygala; Marrtji djawuḻpa'wala miyalkkala), -lili (yuṯalili bathilili), -ŋuru (Yuṯaŋuru bala'ŋuru ŋayi walmana), -galaŋuŋuru (djawuḻpa'walaŋuŋuru miyalkkalaŋuŋuru), -guŋu (miyalkkuŋu djawuḻpa'wuŋu, märrma'wuŋu), instrument -dhu (dharpay yindiy, dharpay weyindhu, lipalipay ḻurrkun'thu, miyalkkala rerrimirriwala).

lessons.title: Possessive adjectives (1): with object of a verb

rules.statement: The -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu form of the Possessive Adjective (Lessons 13-14) is used where the thing or person described has NO suffix: in verbless sentences (Dhuwala guya ŋarraku) and with the subject of an intransitive verb (Ŋarraku Bäpa marrtjina, My father went).

When a Possessive Adjective modifies the OBJECT of a verb the same form is used: Djupandawuygu miyalknha bumara ŋayi (He beat Djupandawuy's wife), Balimaŋgu/Wandjukku/Mawalan'ku/Djäwawa miyalknha bumara ŋayi; Bäpay walalaŋgu dhägir'yurruna djamarrkuḻi'nha (Father punished their children), napurruŋgu/nhanŋu/ŋarraku/nhuŋu.

lessons.title: Possessive adjectives (2): suffix -gala/-kala/-wala

rules.statement: Revise Lessons 13, 14 and 35 (Possessive Adjectives formed by Noun or Personal Pronoun plus -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu). Another form of Possessive Adjective is made by adding suffix -gala/-kala/-wala to Nouns or Personal Pronouns; it is used when the noun described carries a suffix.

With the AGENT of a transitive verb (see Lesson 22): Marmburrgala/-wala miyalkthu ŋanya nhäŋala (Marmburr's wife saw him), Balimaŋgala / Wandjukkala / Djäwawala miyalkthu ŋanya nhäŋala; with pronouns AFTER the head: Bäpay linyalaŋgala dhäwu ŋäkula (Our father heard the news), Bäpay maṉḏaŋgala / nhanukala / ŋarrakala dhäwu ŋäkula.

With noun ending in -lili (Lesson 27): Gäŋu Balimaŋgala/Laklakkala/Lorruwala/Bäpawala wäŋalili (Take it to X's place); Maṉḏaŋgala/Nhanukala/Ŋarrakala dhurrwaralili nhirrpulu (Put it by their/his/my door). With noun ending in -ŋura (Lesson 25): Maṉḏa ga nhina galki Wandjukkala/Djäwawala/ŋarrakala/nhokala wäŋaŋura (They are sitting near X's place). With noun ending in -ŋuru (Lesson 28): Maṉḏa yawirriny'kala/Djäwawala/ŋarrakala/nhokala bala'ŋuru walmana (They came out of X's hut). With noun ending in -dhu/-thu/-yu/-y, instrument (Lesson 33): Walala marrtjina Wandjukkala/Stephengala/Bäyawala ṉakuy (They went in X's canoe); Yaka buny'tjurru nhanukala/ŋarrakala ḻuŋinydhu (Don't smoke (with) his/my pipe).

lessons.title: Derived words (3): combination words

rules.statement: Words can be made by the combination of two other words, hyphenated. Noun+verb → different verb: buku-bakmarama (answer), bäka-bakmarama (take revenge), dha-birrka'yun (question — the verb table gives dhä-birrka'yun), dhuḏi-dhurrparama (follow on behind), gupa-waŋa (talk behind someone else's back), gumurr-waṉḏirri (run to meet), guwaḻ-ṉirr'marama (tempt), mel-gurrupan (show), ŋoy-märrama (annoy). Noun+adjective → different adjective: ḻiya-ḏäl (clever), ḻiya-dhumuk (lawless, dull), buthuru-dhumuk (deaf), matha-dhumuk (dumb), dhakal-gurriri (round island), mel-yalŋgi (considerate), galŋa-ḏäl (mean), ḻiya-räwak (bald), gandarr-ḏumurru (fat), ḻiya-yindi (dwarfed). Noun+adjective → different noun: makarr-yindi (mainland), manaŋa-ḏumurru (thief), nyäḻ'-ḏumurru (liar), djarrma-ḏumurru (scandalmonger). Noun+noun → adjective: dhuwurr-yätj (sinful), ḻiya-ṉinydjiya and ḻiya-ḏaruma (bald).

notes: Combination words are hyphenated; stress often occurs on the first syllable of EACH part (buku-bakmarama); when the first word is only one syllable, stress often occurs on that word alone (dhä-birrka'yun)
At Yirrkala, if the second part of a hyphenated word begins with b or g it is changed to w; if it begins with dh or dj it is changed to y (buku-wakthunmarama for answer)
Some nouns are also adjectives and vice-versa: manaŋa-ḏumurru as noun (Manaŋa-ḏumurruy djaw'yurruna, A thief took it) and as adjective (Manaŋa-ḏumurruy yolŋuy djaw'yurruna, A thieving person took it)
The lesson prints dha-birrka'yun (user confirmed) while the verb table gives dhä-birrka'yun — both printed

lessons.title: Derived words (4): addition or subtraction of -'yun/-'thun

rules.statement: The addition of the suffix -'yun/-'thun to certain nouns, adjectives and adverbs changes them to verbs: galay'yun, yapa'yun, ḏutji'yun (make fire), dhä'yun (open one's mouth), matha'yun (poke out one's tongue), waṉa'yun (wave), ḏiltji'yun (bend over), goŋ'thun (poke with finger), djaḏaw'yun (break of day), munha'yun (become night), rathala'yun (have a headache), ŋalparr'yun (cough), ŋurrtji'yun (blow one's nose), gumurr'yun (meet); ganuŋ'thun (limp), nyäḻ'yun (tell a lie), dhägir'yun/dhäḏir'yun/ṉuŋgatthun (forbid, punish); yaka'yun and bäyŋu'yun (say no), räli'yun (walk forward), bala'yun (walk away), bondi'yun (hurry), bulnha'yun (slow down). -'yun follows vowel, liquid, y or w; -'thun follows nasal.

Conversely, the subtraction of -'yun/-'thun from certain verbs produces adjectives: dhägir'yun → dhägir' (forbidden). Sometimes the verb stem is doubled: ḻapthun → ḻapḻap (open), bakthun → bakpak (broken), ḏaw'yun → ḏaw'ṯaw (broken), ḏapthun → ḏapṯap (clenched); the second syllable devoices after a voiceless stop or glottal (ḏap→ṯap).

notes: nyäḻ' is an adjective (untrue) and also a noun (lie)
In ḏapṯap the second syllable changes from ḏap to ṯap because it follows a voiceless stop; similarly bakpak and ḏaw'ṯaw (glottal stop is voiceless)

lessons.title: Derived words (5): noun plus -buy/-puy/-wuy = adjective

rules.statement: Lesson 8: noun plus -mirri = adjective 'having/possessing' (gapumirri). When suffix -buy/-puy/-wuy is added to a noun ('thing' not 'person') it produces an adjective denoting 'belonging to / for / about': gapupuy describes something which belongs to the sea (gapupuy balanda - sailor). Rules: 1. -buy follows nasals (m/n/ṉ/ny/ŋ). 2. -puy follows stops (p/t/ṯ/tj/k/'). 3. -puy or -wuy follows vowels (a/i/u), vowel plus glottal (a'/i'/u'), liquids (l/ḻ/r/rr), liquids plus glottal (l'/ḻ'/r'/rr') and y, y', w, w'.

Pure adjectives can be used with these derived adjectives; they too must take -buy/-puy/-wuy: Dhuwala gapupuy raypinybuy guya (This is a freshwater fish); Ŋayi dhäwu ḻakaraŋala guyapuy märrma'wuy (He told a story about two fish). raypiny = 'fresh', contrasting with moṉuk 'salt'.

When -buy/-puy/-wuy is added to a Noun which is a person, the infix -galaŋu-/-kalaŋu-/-walaŋu- is inserted: Ŋarra yurru miyalkkalaŋuwuy dhäwu ḻakarama (I'll tell you a story about a woman). Infix form: nasal → -galaŋu(wuy); stop → -kalaŋu(wuy); liquid → -galaŋu/-walaŋu; liquid plus glottal → -kalaŋu/-walaŋu; vowel/vowel plus glottal → -walaŋu(wuy). Added to pronouns: ŋarrakalaŋuwuy, nhokalaŋuwuy (user re-checked: both pronouns in -ŋu-), nhanukalaŋuwuy; ŋalitjalaŋgalaŋuwuy; ŋalinyalaŋgalaŋuwuy, nhumalaŋgalaŋuwuy, maṉḏaŋgalaŋuwuy; ŋalimurruŋgalaŋuwuy; ŋanapurruŋgalaŋuwuy, nhumalaŋgalaŋuwuy, walalaŋgalaŋuwuy. The infix is sometimes pronounced -galaŋa-/-kalaŋa-/-walaŋa- with slight emphasis on the final -a- (yolŋuwalaŋawuy).

Questions and answers: Wanhaŋuwuy dhuwala yolŋu? (Where does this person belong?) - Yirrkalawuy. Dhuwala nhäpuy? (What's this for?) - Guyapuy. Dhäwu ŋayi gana ḻakaraŋala (He told a story) - Nhäpuy? (What about?) - Miyapunuwuy (About a turtle).

Between -puy and -wuy after vowels and liquids the choice is lexical: the book attests gapupuy/guyapuy/ḻukupuy but Yirrkalawuy/munathawuy/miyapunuwuy/buṉapiwuy/djinagawuy/märrma'wuy; attested -wuy mains are stored as sufijoBuy data on the entry and the other form is always offered as an alternative

lessons.title: Derived words (6): numeral adjective plus -mirri = adverb; (7): noun plus -ŋura = adverb

rules.statement: 'I have two knives': 'two' is an adjective (modifies the noun). 'I clapped twice': 'twice' is an adverb (modifies the verb). The suffix -mirri is added to a numeral adjective (one/two/three etc) to form the adverb which tells 'how many times': waŋgany/one → waŋganymirri/once; märrma'/two → märrma'mirri/twice; ḻurrkun'/three, a few → ḻurrkun'mirri/three times, a few times; dharrwa/many → dharrwamirri/many times; nhämunha'/how many? → nhämunha'mirri/how many times? NOTE: the form buku-waŋgany, buku-märrma' etc is also used instead of waŋganymirri, märrma'mirri etc.

Lesson 25 gave Adverbial Expressions of Place from -ŋura added to Things (wäŋaŋura/in the camp). -ŋura added to parts of the body forms Adverbs of Place: ḏiltji/back → ḏiltjiŋura/behind, at the back; gumurr/chest → gumurrŋura/in front; ŋoy/seat of emotions → ŋoyŋura/underneath; ḏämbu/head → ḏämbuŋura/above; gali'/side → gali'ŋura/at the side; dhuḏi/buttocks → dhuḏiŋura/at the bottom. NOTE: -ŋura is added to a Thing, -gala/-kala/-wala is added to a Person.

lessons.title: Negative of same-day-past

rules.statement: Lesson 16: the same-day-past (tertiary form) is used for any event which occurred today, in the indefinite past, or in the far distant past (Ŋayi dharpuŋala - He speared it). When the same-day-past is made NEGATIVE, the QUATERNARY form of the verb is used, with yaka or bäyŋu. Group 1 remains the same throughout (Ŋarra gana bäyŋu djäma - I didn't work). Group 2: primary -i, quaternary adds -nya(ra) (marrtjinya). Group 3: primary -a, adds -nha(ra) (ḻukanha). Group 4: primary -rri, drops it and adds -nya(ra) (waṉḏinya). Group 5: primary -un, adds -a(ra) (ḻupthuna). Group 6: primary -an, adds -a(ra) (gurrupana). Group 7: primary -ma changes to -nha plus optional -ra (nhänha). Group 8: -gama/-kama changes to -ganha/-kanha plus optional -(ra) (dhiŋganha). Irregular: ganarrthanha, ŋayathanha, bunha, ŋänha. NOTES: 1. the long quaternary in -ra is sometimes used but very often -ra is omitted. 2. the continuous aspect also uses the quaternary form when negative: Yaka ŋayi buny'tjuna (He didn't smoke), Yaka ŋayi gana buny'tjuna (He wasn't smoking). 3-4. In Yirrkala dialects (and often at Elcho, influenced by Yirrkala or by Dhaŋu'mirri speakers of 'weak' Gupapuyŋu) the tertiary form with yaka/bäyŋu is more usual: Ŋarra yaka nhäŋala (I didn't see). 5. bäyŋu is often used instead of yaka.

notes: The book prints every quaternary with optional (ra): marrtjinya(ra) etc; the engine renders the short form as main with the -ra long form as an alternative

The book alternates yaka-first, subject-first and bäyŋu orders freely across the sections; the engine renders subject + yaka + quaternary as main and offers the fronted yaka/bäyŋu orders as alternatives
'I didn't reach/touch/hold (it)' transcribed with 'touch' for composition; reach/hold are the same ŋayathama

lessons.title: Derived words (8): verb plus -mirri = noun

rules.statement: Like English -er (work → worker), the suffix -mirri added to the SHORT QUATERNARY form of a verb produces a noun meaning 'person who performs the action': djäma → djämamirri worker; djäka/djäga → djäkamirri, djägamirri guardian, caretaker; wukirri → wukirrimirri scribe, writer; dhuḻ'yun → bala'-dhuḻ'yunamirri housebuilder, carpenter; guŋga'yun → guŋga'yunamirri helper; ŋamaŋamayun → ŋamaŋamayunamirri maker; buny'tjun → buny'tjunamirri smoker; malthun → malthunamirri follower; bathan → ŋatha-bathanamirri cook; gurrupan → gurrupanamirri giver, medicine-gurrupanamirri nurse; bäy-ḻakarama → bäy-ḻakaranhamirri forgiver; ḻiya-ḻupmarama → ḻiya-ḻupmaranhamirri baptizer; bakmarama → ḻirra-bakmaranhamirri dentist; märrama → rrupiya-märranhamirri money collector, mali-märranhamirri photographer; gäma → dhäwu-gänhamirri messenger; marŋgikuma → marŋgikunhamirri teacher; walŋakuma → walŋakunhamirri saviour, healer; burrmiḏiyama → burrmiḏiyanhamirri peacemaker; waṉakulama → waṉakulanhamirri guide; guwaḻ-ṉirr'marama → guwaḻ-ṉirr'maranhamirri tempter. NOTES: 1. at Yirrkala the long quaternary in -ra is used: ḻiya-ḻupmaranharamirri. 2. in some cases -mirri is added to the verb STEM: djawarrkthun preach → djawarrkmirri preacher. 3. see Lesson 40 for the quaternary form (the book's own cross-reference — confirmed; the quaternary is taught in Lesson 41). 4. pure nouns compound with the derived nouns: ŋatha-bathanamirri person who cooks food, mali-märranhamirri person who takes photos. 5. a rarer form adds -yŋu to the short quaternary: bokman create → bokmanayŋu creator.

notes: The compound and irregular agent nouns are stored as lexical entries with the gups as printed (including medicine-gurrupanamirri with the English word medicine); the productive rule is also implemented mechanically: an unknown English -er noun or Spanish -dor(a) noun whose base resolves to a known verb derives quaternary+mirri at runtime (dancer → giritjinyamirri, fumador → buny'tjunamirri)
The dynamically derived nouns carry the Yirrkala long form (IV+ra+mirri) as an alternate base

lessons.title: Derived words (9): verb plus -mirri = adjective

rules.statement: The Lesson 42 derivation (quaternary + -mirri) also behaves as an adjective: djämamirri miyalk working woman — nouns and adjectives often overlap in Gupapuyŋu. Further examples: manaŋirri → manaŋinyamirri yolŋu person who steals; waṉḏirri → waṉḏinyamirri yolŋu; giritjirri → giritjinyamirri yolŋu; nyäḻ'yun → nyäḻ'yunamirri yolŋu person who lies; biṉdharr'yun → biṉdharr'yunamirri miyalk woman who swears; gaḻ'yun → gaḻ'yunamirri yothu baby who crawls; djaṉ'tjaṉdhun → djaṉ'tjaṉdhunamirri yothu toddler; buṯthun → buṯthunamirri warrakan bird which flies; milkuma → milkunhamirri mitjiyaŋ show boat; nhäma → nhänhamirri mala spectators; ŋuthanmarama → ŋuthanmaranhamirri ŋatha food which makes one grow; nhuman → nhumanamirri waṯu dog which sniffs and smells around. NOTES: 1. adjectives because they modify a noun; the English translation is not always an adjective. 2. other expressions exist: manaŋinyamirri yolŋu / manaŋa-ḏumurru thief (Lesson 37). 3. sometimes -mirri attaches to the verb STEM: baba'yun (bawa'yun) be silly → baba'mirri (bawa'mirri) silly, stupid. 4. at Yirrkala -mirri is added to the long quaternary in -ra: manaŋinyaramirri.
Section A cites 'Lesson 41' for the noun derivation (user confirmed: that derivation is Lesson 42; the book's cross-references here are shifted by one, like note 3 of Lesson 42 citing Lesson 40).

notes: The adjective entries carry natural single-word Spanish forms (volador, gateador, mirón...) because the book's English glosses are relative clauses the engine does not parse

lessons.title: Verb plus -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu: djäl/marŋgi/purpose

rules.statement: Just as -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu is added to nouns, it can be added to quaternary forms of verbs. The LONG quaternary form is always used, and as this ends in a vowel (-a) the suffix is -wa (at Yirrkala -wu). djäl puts the suffix on to the action desired (Lesson 15 put it on the thing desired): Ŋarra djäl djämawa (I want to work — group 1 uses the plain stem), wukirriwa, marrtjinyarawa, gärrinyarawa, ḻukanharawa, ŋorranharawa, roŋiyinyarawa, giritjinyarawa, buḻ'yunarawa, ḻupthunarawa, bathanarawa, gurrupanarawa, nhänharawa, ḻakaranharawa, dhiŋganharawa, gurrukanharawa, ŋayathanharawa, ŋänharawa. NOTE: djäma is a noun as well as a verb, so Ŋarra djäl djämawa is 'I want work' or 'I want to work'. marŋgi works the same way for the action known: Ŋarra marŋgi djämawa (I know how to work), wukirriwa, giritjinyarawa, buny'tjunarawa.

The same suffix on verbs indicates purpose (Lesson 31 showed it on nouns): Ŋayi marrtjina bothurruwa (He went in order to count), waŋanharawa, manaŋinyarawa (gloss printed 'in order to seal' (book typo for steal, confirmed)), guŋga'yunarawa, ŋäŋ'thunarawa, gurrupanarawa, nhänharawa, dharpunharawa, märranharawa, dhiŋganharawa. When a verb AND a noun or pronoun together denote the thing desired/known/the purpose, BOTH take the suffix: Ŋarra djäl gapuwa ḻukanharawa (I want to drink water); Ŋarra djäl Djäwawa nhänharawa; Ŋarra djäl manikaygu ŋänharawa; Ŋarra nhuŋu djäl marrtjinyarawa (I want you to go); Ŋarra nhanŋu djäl ḏar'ṯaryunarawa (I want him to sing); Ŋarra marŋgi ŋathawa bathanarawa (I know how to cook food); Ŋarra marŋgi bathiwa bunharawa (I know how to make a basket); Ŋayi marrtjina miyalkku djaw'yunarawa (He went for the purpose of running away with a woman); Ŋayi marrtjina märriyaŋgu märranharawa (He went to get the gun); [name] dhiŋgaŋala ŋarraku walŋakunharawa (died to save me), nhuŋu walŋakunharawa (the book's example sentence uses a religious figure, omitted by request — the dative beneficiary + purpose infinitive composes with any name). NOTES: 1. Ŋarra nhuŋu djäl guŋga'yunarawa is ambiguous (I want to help you / I want you to help); periphrases disambiguate: Ŋarra djäl ŋarra dhu nhuna guŋga'yun; Ŋarra nhuŋu djäl nhe yurru guŋga'yun. 2. Suffixes -lili and -gala/-kala/-wala do NOT become -gu: Ŋarra djäl wäŋalili marrtjinyarawa (I want to go to the camp). F. Adjectives modifying the nouns also take the suffix: Ŋayi djäl romgu manymakku ŋayathanharawa (He wants to keep the good way).

G. Expressions of purpose have been adverbial (Ŋayi marrtjina gapuwa — 'for water' tells why he came); they can also be ADJECTIVAL, modifying a noun, formed the same way: Dhuwala djurra' nhänharawa (This book is for looking at — djurra' — the book uses djurra' and djorra' interchangeably (user confirmed)); Dhuwala djurra' wukirriwa; Dhuwala nyoka buny'tjunarawa (This crab-claw is for smoking); Dhuwala yiki mitthunarawa (This knife is for cutting); Dhuwala djimiṉḏi guyawa barrtjunarawa (This spear is for spearing fish); Dhuwala guṉḏa warraga'wa wutthunarawa (This stone is for beating cycads — guṉḏa (guṉḏa/gunḏa both printed in the book — user confirmed)); Dhuwala djambaka ŋathawa bathanarawa (This tin is for cooking food); Dhuwala ḏakul gurthawa djatthunarawa (This axe is for chopping firewood). Question: Nhaku dhuwala?/Nhäku? (What's this for?) Answer: Guyawa barrtjunarawa (For spearing fish). NOTES: 1. stress falls mainly on the first syllable with slight emphasis on -ra (ḻupthunarawa). 2. word order in a sentence is not fixed.

lessons.title: Verb plus -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu: English infinitive

rules.statement: The English infinitive (to go/to cook/to see/to say) is usually translated by the long quaternary form plus -wa (Lesson 44 covered djäl, marŋgi and purpose). After any finite verb: Ŋarra gorana ḻakaranharawa (I was ashamed to tell); Ŋarra barrarina roŋiyinyarawa (I was frightened to return/of returning); Ŋarra moŋala ḻupthunarawa (I forgot to wash); Ŋarra guyaŋana manaŋinyarawa (I thought to steal/of stealing); Ŋarra barrarina wutthunarawa gatapaŋawa (I was frightened to shoot the buffalo); Ŋarra moŋala djuy'yunarawa (I forgot to send the things). NOTE 1: gora/be ashamed, barrarirri/be frightened and mukthun/be quiet are verbs in Gupapuyŋu.

With guŋga'yun (help someone to) and waŋa (tell someone to): Ŋarranha guŋga'yurru dhuḻ'yunarawa (Help me to build it); Ŋarranha guŋga'yurru djämawa (Help me to do the work); Yapay ŋanya guŋga'yurruna djurra'wa wukirriwa (Sister helped him to write a letter — djurra' as printed); Yapay ŋanya guŋga'yurruna ŋathawa bathanarawa (Sister helped him to cook the food); Ŋarra ŋanya waŋana ḻupthunarawa (I told him to wash), mukthunarawa (to be quiet), galkunarawa (to wait), guŋga'yunarawa (to help), roŋiyinyarawa (to return); Ŋayi nhuna waŋana girri'wa rurrguyunarawa (He told you to wash the clothes), yothuwa djäkawa (to mind the baby), rrupiyawa bothurruwa (to count the money), dhukungu djalkthunarawa (to throw away the rubbish), gurthawa dhaŋalkunharawa (to light a fire).

NOTE 2: often the quaternary plus -wa is NOT used after 'try' and 'start': Ŋarra birrka'yurruna bathara (I tried to cook it — Lit. I tried cooked it; bathara = the TERTIARY of bathan (user asked: bathara III vs bathanara long-IV are two distinct forms, both in verbs.json — try/start takes the tertiary)); Ŋarra ŋurru-djirr'yurruna ḻupthurruna (I started to wash — Lit. I started washed, tertiary form). NOTE 3: at Yirrkala (and sometimes Milingimbi and Elcho) rurrwuyun is used instead of rurrguyun, and ŋurru-yirr'yun instead of ŋurru-djirr'yun.

The infinitive often follows an adjective; Gupapuyŋu uses the long quaternary plus -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu: Dhuwala guya manymak ḻukanharawa (This fish is good to eat); Dhuwala guya walŋa ḻukanharawa (fresh enough to eat); Dhuwala guya ḏulki ḻukanharawa (too rotten to eat); Dhuwala yiki djinbulk mitthunarawa (sharp enough to cut); Dhuwala yiki dhumuk mitthunarawa (too blunt to cut); Dhuwala ḏamba gurrukanharawa (light enough to carry); Dhuwala ŋoṉuŋ gurrukanharawa (too heavy to carry). NOTES: the English often needs 'enough' or 'too' added; the infinitive can be replaced by 'for...ing'. G TO REITERATE: the infinitive is usually '...arawa' (Ŋayi marrtjina nhänharawa, Ŋarra djäl marrtjinyarawa, Ŋayi gorana roŋiyinyarawa); invariable verbs bothurru/djäma/wukirri merely add -wa (Ŋarra djäl wukirriwa). The DIRECT OBJECT of an infinitive takes the same suffix: manaŋinyarawa mapuwa (to steal an egg), ŋäŋ'thunarawa Bäpawa (to ask Bäpa), ḻukanharawa warrakangu (to eat meat), märranharawa maŋal'ku (to get a spearthrower).

lessons.title: Verb plus -ŋura, -lili, -ŋuru, -y, -puy/wuy

rules.statement: The suffixes -ŋura, -lili, -ŋuru, -y and -puy/-wuy can also be added to a verb (the SHORT quaternary form; section A cites 'Lessons 43 and 44' — the book's own cross-reference (confirmed): 44-45). -ŋura on the short quaternary produces an Adverbial Expression of Place: Q. Wanha Yipiṯi? A. Djämaŋura (At work), Wukirriŋura (At school, lit. at write), Buḻ'yunaŋura (At play), Ḻupthunaŋura (Washing), Barrtjunaŋura (Hunting/Fishing), Ŋathaŋura ḻukanhaŋura (Eating his breakfast — the object also takes -ŋura), Gurthaŋura djatthunaŋura (Chopping firewood), Girri'ŋura rurrguyunaŋura (Washing his clothes).

-lili on the short quaternary produces Movement Towards: Q. Nhäkurru? (Where to?) A. Djämalili (To the place where I shall work), Wukirrilili, Buḻ'yunalili, Ḻupthunalili, Ŋorranhalili, Guyalili barrtjunalili (to spear fish — the object also takes -lili).

-ŋuru on the short quaternary produces Movement Away: Ŋayi rur'yurruna dhiŋganhaŋuru (He arose from the dead, lit. from die), ŋorranhaŋuru (from sleep), ḻiyamirriyanhaŋuru (from prayer, lit. from pray); Ŋayi roŋiyina ḻupthunaŋuru (He returned from washing), giritjinyaŋuru (from dancing), buḻ'yunaŋuru (from play), guyaŋuru barrtjunaŋuru (from fishing — object -ŋuru too), djämaŋuru (from work).

E. Lesson 33 showed Thing plus -dhu/-thu/-yu/-y as an Adverbial Expression of Instrument (dharpay with a stick, mitjiyaŋdhu by boat). The same suffix can be added to the LONG Quaternary Verb form; as it always ends in a vowel (-a) the suffix will be -y (at Yirrkala, -yu): Yothunha ŋayi mukmaraŋala waŋanharay (She quietened the baby by talking), ḏar'ṯaryunaray (by singing — retroflex dots confirmed by user), ŋaminiy gurrupanaray (by giving it milk — ŋamini/ŋämini — both spellings printed (user confirmed)); the book's fourth example (showing a person to his enemies by kissing, walkunharay as printed (user confirmed; wälkuma's table would give wälkunharay)) uses religious figures, omitted by request — the frame [name]-nha milkuŋala [name]-dhu miriŋuwala wälkunharay composes with any names.

F. Lesson 39 showed Thing plus -buy/-puy/-wuy and Person plus -galaŋuwuy/-kalaŋuwuy/-walaŋuwuy denoting 'about'. The same suffix on the short Quaternary form produces an Adjective or Adjectival Expression denoting 'about': Dhäwu ŋayi ḻakaraŋala miyapunuwuy dharpunhawuy (He told a story about spearing a turtle); Dhäwi ŋayi ḻakaraŋala bäpipuy bunhawuy (about killing a snake — Dhäwi as printed twice (user confirmed; dhäwu elsewhere — book-internal variant)); the third example (the story of a person dying: [name]-walaŋuwuy dhiŋganhawuy — a person subject of the gerund takes the comitative infix) uses a religious figure, omitted by request.

G. Lesson 39 also showed Thing plus -buy/-puy/-wuy denoting 'for' (mulmupuy bathi, a box for hay). The same suffix on the Short Quaternary Form produces an Adjective or Adjectival Expression denoting 'for'. Pointing at a spade, a pipe, a fish spear, a piece of fencing wire, a refrigerator and asking Nhäpuy dhuwali? (What's that for?): Dhawaraŋbuy belanhawuy (For digging holes — dhawaraŋ hole (user confirmed; djetji is the L8 word — synonyms)), Ŋarali'puy buny'tjunawuy (For smoking tobacco), Guyapuy barrtjunawuy (For spearing fish), Ḻuŋinybuy yirrpanawuy (For cleaning pipes, lit. for scraping pipes used for smoking), Guyapuy ŋorranhawuy (For fish to lie in). NOTES: 1. these denote purpose, so -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu may be used instead (Lesson 44 Section G — cited as 'Lesson 44, Section G', consistent with the cross-references shifted elsewhere): Q. Nhäpuy dhuwala? A. Guyapuy barrtjunawuy / Q. Nhaku~Nhäku dhuwala? A. Guyawa barrtjunarawa. 2. Either -wuy or -puy can be added to the Quaternary Verb Form because it ends in -a. 3. At Yirrkala the Long Quaternary form is always used: ḻupthunaraŋura. 4. Word order in a sentence is not fixed.

lessons.title: Behaviour of certain verbs

rules.statement: A-H. A family of INTRANSITIVE verbs takes no suffix on the subject (Lesson 24) and puts -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu on the Thing or Person the action is directed at: ḻarruma search/seek/look for (Bäpa gana ḻarruŋala märriyaŋgu / nhuŋu), galkun wait (Stephen yurru Balimaŋgu galkun / maṉḏaŋgu — yurru printed for the future particle throughout this lesson, dhu elsewhere), gitkitthun laugh at (Yaka gitkitthurru Yapawa / ŋarraku), malthun accompany/follow/go with (Djamarrkuḻi' ga Balimaŋgu malthun / nhanŋu), djäka~djäga look after/care for/guard (Yol ga djäka yothuwa? / ŋathawa?), wäthun call/call out to (Bäya yawirriny'ku wäthurruna, Bäya nhumalaŋgu wäthurruna), ŋamathirri love/like/welcome ([subject] ga ŋamathirri ŋilimurruŋu / walalaŋgu / djamarrkuḻi'wa — the book's subject is a religious figure, omitted by request; ŋilimurruŋu as printed — ŋilimurruŋu and ŋalimurruŋgu are two versions of the same form (user confirmed); the engine offers both; the verb table glosses ŋamathirri 'improve'), barrarirri be/become frightened of (Yothu gana barrarina waṯuwa / waltjaṉgu (user re-checked: retroflex ṉ — waltjaṉ + -gu, matching the engine)).

I. bäy-ḻakarama (forgive/overlook) is TRANSITIVE: -dhu/-thu/-yu/-y on the Agent (Lesson 22), dative on the person forgiven: [agent]-dhu yurru nhuŋu bäy-ḻakarama yätjkurru dhuwurr (will forgive your sin — the book's agent is a religious figure, omitted by request). NOTE: 'sin' (yätjkurru dhuwurr) is often omitted — the verb stays transitive. NOTE 2: sometimes -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu is added to the Thing forgiven: Ŋayi yurru bäy-ḻakarama yätjkurruwa dhuwurrwu (user re-checked: dhuwurr 'sin/way'). The verb table (page 52) marks bäy-ḻakarama Vin, this lesson says Transitive (engine follows the lesson).

J. waŋa (speak/talk/tell/say) is Transitive OR Intransitive. With -nha on the Person addressed the verb is transitive and the Agent (the speaker) takes -dhu/-thu/-yu/-y: Bäpay waŋana Stephennha. With -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu or -gala/-kala/-wala on the person addressed the verb is intransitive and the subject takes no suffix: Bäpa waŋana Stephengu/Stephengala.

K. ḻakarama (tell/say) is Transitive: -dhu/-thu/-yu/-y on the Agent, -nha on the Person told ON or ABOUT (Wandjukthu ḻakaraŋala Raymannha / nhuna); -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu or -gala/-kala/-wala on the person TOLD (the hearer): Wandjukthu Bäpawa/Bäpawala ḻakaraŋala; Wandjuk ŋarraku/ŋarrakala ḻakaraŋala (printed WITHOUT the agent suffix on Wandjuk (confirmed by user) — the engine keeps Wandjukthu). In 'I'll tell Bäpa on you' -nha goes on the person told on and -gala/-kala/-wala (not -gu) on the person told: Ŋarra yurru nhuna ḻakarama Bäpawala; Ŋarra yurru ŋanya ḻakarama Bäpawala.

L-M. gurrupan (give), djuy'yun and yänguma (send), gäma (bring/take) are Transitive with -dhu/-thu/-yu/-y on the Agent. The RECIPIENT takes -nha or -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu if the thing given/sent/brought is his to keep: Stephendhu yiki gurrupara Djäwanha/Djäwawa; Yambalnha/Yambalgu; Djäway nhanŋu girri' djuy'yurruna (sent him some things for himself); Walala Yapawa guya gäŋala (brought a fish to Sister for herself). The recipient takes -gala/-kala/-wala if it is NOT his to keep but to return or give to someone else: Ŋarra djurra' gurrupara Djäwawala / Yambalgala (djurra'/djorra' both fine — user confirmed); Djamarrkuḻi'nha gäŋu Yapawala (Take the children to Sister). Wife-giving: Walala miyalk gurrupara Djapala'wa/Djapala'nha — usually no suffix on miyalk though a person (cf. Lesson 19); with the woman's name, -nha: Walala Goŋay'nha gurrupara Djapala'nha/Djapala'wa (NOTE: -nha on both is unambiguous — a woman is always given to a man). NOTE: word order is not fixed.

lessons.title: Transitive suffix -marama

rules.statement: A-B. Every verb ending in -marama is Transitive (except combination words like buku-bakmarama; see Lesson 22 — don't confuse -marama with märrama get/take). Some intransitive verbs become transitive by adding -marama; the result falls into Group 7 and behaves like all verbs in -ma. The base depends on the group of the INTRANSITIVE: Groups 2, 3, 4, 7 and 8 add -marama to the SHORT Quaternary form (gärri → gärrinyamarama let/make go in: Djäwa gärrina / Djäway ŋanya gärrinyamaraŋala; nhina → nhinanhamarama make sit: Balimaŋ nhinana / Balimaŋdhu walalanha nhinanhamaraŋala; gulŋiyirri → gulŋiyinyamarama let go in: Walala gulŋiyina / Walala gulŋiyinyamaraŋala djamarrkuḻi'nha; dhiŋgama → dhiŋganhamarama make die — the book's H example uses a religious figure, omitted by request). Group 5 adds -marama to the verb STEM (ḻupthun → ḻupmarama wash: Guyumul ḻupthurruna / Guyumulyu ḻupmaraŋala yothuna — confirmed as printed (variant of yothunha); mukthun → mukmarama quieten: Lorru mukthurruna / Lorruy ŋanya mukmaraŋala; bakthun → bakmarama break: Tractor bakthurruna / Raymandhu tractor bakmaraŋala). Group 6 adds -marama to the PRIMARY form (ḻithan get warm/dry → ḻithanmarama dry/warm: Ŋarra yurru ḻithan / Girri' ŋarra yurru ḻithanmarama; ŋuthan grow → ŋuthanmarama make grow, bring up: Yothu yurru ŋuthan / Märi'mirriŋuy yurru ŋuthanmarama yothunha).

I. Some irregular transitive forms: roŋiyirri (go/return) → roŋanmarama give/take back (Bäya roŋiyirri / Bäyay djurra' roŋanmaraŋala — djurra' as printed, djorra' elsewhere); barrarirri (be/become frightened) → barrarikukuma frighten (Mawuyul barrarina / Mawuyulyu ŋarranha barrarikukuŋala). NOTES: 1. not every transitive verb ends in -marama (ḻuka eat). 2. sometimes two entirely different verbs mark intransitive vs transitive: biŋga'yun wake up / dhirr'yun wake someone (Ŋarra biŋga'yurruna / Ŋarra ŋanya dhirr'yurruna); nhära burn (intr.) / bathan burn (tr.) (Gurtha gana nhärana / Gurthay ŋarranha bathara). 3. sometimes the SAME verb is both: nhuman smell (Gatapaŋa barrpa' ga nhuman — the buffalo meat smells bad / Gatapaŋay ga mulmu nhuman — the buffalo is smelling the grass). 4. dhaḻ'yun and dhaḻ'marama (shut) are both transitive; gulkthun and gulkmarama (cut) are both transitive. 5. at Yirrkala: (a) the LONG Quaternary would probably be used instead of the Short (groups 2, 3, 4, 7, 8); (b) with group 5 verbs -marama is added to the PRIMARY form, not the stem: ḻupthunmarama. 6. word order is not fixed.

lessons.title: Derived words (10): adjective plus -dhirri/-thirri/-yirri intransitive verb

rules.statement: A-E. Adjective + -dhirri/-thirri/-yirri produces an INTRANSITIVE verb meaning 'becoming'. B: after a nasal, -dhirri (borum→borumdhirri become ripe, rakuny→rakunydhirri become dead, ŋonuŋ→ŋonuŋdhirri become heavy — printed ŋonuŋ (user confirmed; ŋoṉuŋ in L45 — book-internal variants); dhaŋaŋ→dhaŋaŋdhirri become full, nyumukuṉiny→nyumukuṉinydhirri become little). C: after a stop, -thirri (manymak→manymakthirri become good/get better, ḏarrtjalk→ḏarrtjalkthirri become clean, djurruk→djurrukthirri become wet, maḏakarritj→maḏakarritjthirri become angry, mutitj→mutitjthirri become calm of water etc). D: after a liquid or -y or -w, usually -thirri (ḏäl→ḏälthirri become strong/hard, djäl→djälthirri be/become desirous, djaŋŋarr→djaŋŋarrthirri be/become hungry, bambay→bambaythirri be blind/shut eyes); NOTE sometimes -yirri after a liquid: guyiŋarr→guyiŋarryirri, guyiŋarrthirri become cold. E: after a vowel or vowel plus glottal stop, either -thirri or -yirri (dhunupa→dhunupayirri become straight, dharraḏa→dharraḏayirri become still, muḏaḏa→muḏaḏayirri become quiet, ḏumurru→ḏumurruyirri become big, djawuḻpa'→djawuḻpa'yirri/-thirri become old, bukumunha→bukumunhayirri become dark, djarrpi'→djarrpi'yirri/-thirri become crooked, mulka'→mulka'thirri become dry, marŋgi→marŋgithirri learn, yindi→yindithirri become big, walŋa→walŋathirri become well/get better, yalŋgi→yalŋgithirri become weak/soft, yuṯa→yuṯathirri become new, dharrwa→dharrwathirri become many/increase).

F. Two irregular forms: ŋamakurru (good, well) → ŋamathirri become good/well (get better); yätjkurru (bad) → yätjirri be/become bad. G. All verbs in this Lesson fall into Group 3 (ending in -rri). Examples: Dharraḏayi! (Be still! — become still); Maŋutji bambaythi! (Shut your eyes!); Yothu rakunydhina (The baby died); Ŋarra djäl walŋathinyarawa (I want to live/get better); Yol maḏakarritjthina? (Who became/got angry?).

lessons.title: Derived words (11): adjective plus -guma/-kuma/-yama transitive verb

rules.statement: A-B. Adjective + -guma/-kuma/-yama produces a TRANSITIVE verb meaning 'making'. Rules: after a nasal, -guma; after a stop, -kuma; after -y/-w/liquid, -kuma; after a vowel, either -kuma or -yama. Examples: rakuny→rakunyguma make dead (kill), dhaŋaŋ→dhaŋaŋguma make full (fill), ḏarrtjalk→ḏarrtjalkkuma make clean, manymak→manymakkuma make good, ḏäl→ḏälkuma make strong, bambay→bambaykuma make blind, marŋgi→marŋgikuma teach/inform, walŋa→walŋakuma save/heal, yuṯa→yuṯakuma make new, dhunupa→dhunupayama straighten/make right, burrmiḏi→burrmiḏiyama make peaceful.

C-D. Two irregular forms: ŋamakurru → ŋamathama make (something) good or well; yätjkurru → yätjama make bad, spoil. All verbs in this Lesson fall into Group 7 (ending in -ma). The book's usage examples ([agent]-dhu nhuna yurru ḏarrtjalkkuma / walŋakuma / ḏälkuma — will cleanse/save/strengthen you; [agent]-y ŋanya ŋamathaŋala / yuṯakuŋala / marŋgikuŋala — made him feel better / made him new / taught him) use religious figures, omitted by request — the frames compose with any subject. Imperative examples: Dhuwala mulka'kuŋu (Dry this); Dhuwala dhunupayaŋu (Straighten this). NOTE: the suffix -dhama/-thama is used in some dialects instead of -guma/-kuma.

notes: Same productive mechanism as Lesson 49 with tipo kuma (nasal→guma, stop/liquid→kuma, vowel→kuma with -yama alternative; sufijoKuma pins dhunupa→yama); the group-7 paradigm (-ma/-ŋu/-ŋala/-nha) is synthesized unless verbs.json attests the lemma (walŋakuma, marŋgikuma, ŋamathama, yätjama are real entries)

lessons.title: Possessive adjectives (3) with infix -galaŋu/-kalaŋu/-walaŋu

rules.statement: A-D. Lessons 13-14 gave possessive adjectives with unsuffixed nouns (Dhuwala guya Djäwawa/ŋarraku), Lesson 35 with -nha nouns (Ŋayi bumara Djäwawa miyalknha), Lesson 36 with -ŋura/-lili nouns (Gäŋu Djäwawala wäŋalili). When the noun carries -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu, the possessive adjective takes the SAME suffix with the infix -galaŋu-/-kalaŋu-/-walaŋu- inserted (Lesson 39 Section I gives the form rules). E after djäl: Ŋarra djäl märriyaŋgu Stephengalaŋuwa / Bäyawalaŋuwa / nhokalaŋuwa (I want Stephen's/Bäya's/your gun). F after marŋgi: Ŋayi marŋgi ŋarrakalaŋuwa yapawa / nhanukalaŋuwa yapawa / maṉḏaŋgalaŋuwa yapawa (He knows my/her/their sister). G purpose (Lesson 31): Ŋarra marrtjina Djäwawalaŋuwa ṉakuwa nhänharawa (I went to see Djäwa's canoe — ṉaku canoe; the engine's canoe is lipalipa), Wandjukkalaŋuwa, litjalaŋgalaŋuwa (our). H after the Lesson 47 dative verbs: Ŋayi gana djäka girri'wa ŋarrakalaŋuwa (looking after my things), malthurruna Bäpawa ŋarrakalaŋuwa (went with my father), galkurruna yapawa ŋarrakalaŋuwa (waiting for my sister), ḻarruŋala yikiwa ŋarrakalaŋuwa (looking for my knife). I with another possessive adjective: Dhuwala yiki ŋarrakalaŋuwa Bäpawa (This is my father's knife), Bäyawalaŋuwa Bäpawa, Lorruwalaŋuwa Bäpawa. NOTE: word order in sentence is not fixed.

lessons.title: Possessive adjectives (3) cont. with infix -galaŋu-/-kalaŋu-/-walaŋu-

rules.statement: The same infix appears before every other case suffix. A before -gala/-kala/-wala (Lessons 26, 27, 33): Ŋayi ga nhina miyalkkala Djäwawalaŋuwala / ŋarrakalaŋuwala (sitting with Djäwa's/my wife); Gurrupulu Raymangalaŋuwala miyalkkala / nhanukalaŋuwala miyalkkala (gave it to Rayman's/his wife — Gurrupulu — confirmed by user as printed). B before -guŋu/-kuŋu/-wuŋu (Lesson 30): [name]-wuŋu [pron]-galaŋuwuŋu (this is a gift from our —; the book's example is religious, omitted by request; note: sometimes shortened to -ŋgala). C before -buy/-puy/-wuy (Lesson 39): Ŋarra dhu nhuŋu dhäwu ḻakarama mapu'puy balandawalaŋuwuy (I'll tell you about the white people's eggs); the second example is religious, omitted by request. D before -ŋuru (Lessons 28, 29): Yarrkthurru bala'ŋuru ŋarrakalaŋuŋuru (Move away from my hut — the engine orders the possessor first, word order not fixed), Yarrkthurru miyalkkalaŋuŋuru nhanukalaŋuŋuru (from his wife); sometimes shortened to ŋarrakala or nhanukala (compare Lesson 36 Section F). NOTES: 1. Lesson 39 Section I gives the infix form rules. 2. Word order in sentence is not fixed.

notes: D is COMPOSED: the ablative possessor now renders the full infixed form as main (ŋarrakalaŋuŋuru) with the Lesson 36 shortened -kala as the alternative — the three Lesson 36 regression assertions were updated accordingly (both forms book-attested)

lessons.title: Adverbial expression (7): movement along/through, suffix -gurru/-kurru/-wurru

rules.statement: A. -gurru/-kurru/-wurru usually denotes movement 'along' or 'through' (and other uses, G). Form rules: -gurru after nasals (m/n/ṉ/ny/ŋ); -kurru after stops (p/t/ṯ/tj/k/'); -kurru or -wurru after vowels, vowel+glottal, liquids (l/ḻ/r/rr), liquid+glottal, y/y'/w/w'. B Thing + kurru: Ḏiltjikurru ŋarra marrtjina gana (I was walking through the bush — gana printed after the verb (confirmed — yesterday-continuous, free word order)), Mulmukurru (grass), Gapukurru (water), Dhukarrkurru (road/path), Dhurrwarakurru (gate/door). C Person + kurru requires the infix -galaŋu/-kalaŋu/-walaŋu (the book's example is religious, omitted by request: [pron] yurru [name]-ku marŋgithirri [name]-walaŋuwurru — we shall learn about X through Y). D adjectives agree: Napurru ga marrtji manymakkurru dhukarrkurru / yätjkurrukurru dhukarrkurru / wiripuŋuwurru dhukarrkurru (along the good/bad/another road — Napurru as printed (user re-checked: initial N — shortened ŋanapurru)). E possessive adjectives with -kurru heads take the infix (the book's examples are religious — [name]-walaŋuwurru dhuwurrkurru, we shall go along X's way — omitted by request; nhokalaŋuwurru your way).

F. -kurru/-wurru is occasionally added to the SHORT quaternary verb form (cf. Lessons 44/45/46), best translated 'during' or 'while': Ŋayi gana buḻ'yurruna wukirriwurru (playing during school, lit. while writing); Ŋayi gana guyaŋana ŋanya djämakurru (thinking of her while working); Ŋarra maḻŋ'maraŋala ŋanya ŋorranhawurru (I found/met him during sleep, i.e. dreamt about him). G. often used where English says neither 'along' nor 'through': Warrakan ga buṯthun garrwarkurru (A bird is flying above); Buḻ'yurru barrkukurru! (Play a long way away!); Yaka wapthurru ḻoḻukurru! (Don't jump over the fence); Bäpa ga waŋa djimiṉḏi kurru (talking on the wireless — printed as two words: djimiṉḏi kurru (user confirmed)); Ŋayi ga waŋa yolŋuwurru mathakurru (speaking the native language); Ŋarra dhu marrtji walalaŋgalaŋuwurru (I'll go with them); Walala marrtjina gumurrkurru nhanukalaŋuwurru (They passed in front of him); Walukurru ŋarra gana gäthura marrtjina (I was walking in the sun today). NOTE: word order is not fixed.

lessons.title: This

rules.statement: A. 'This' is an adjective and AGREES with the noun it qualifies — but instead of attaching the suffix it completely changes form. B. THIS = DHUWALA with an unsuffixed noun or -nha: Dhuwala guya ŋarraku (verbless); Dhuwala miyalk marrtjina (intransitive subject); Ŋarra nhäŋala dhuwala miyalknha (transitive object). C. THIS = DHIYAKU with -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu: Ŋarra dhiyaku djäl guyawa (I want this fish); Ŋarra yaka marŋgi dhiyaku yolŋuwa (I don't know this person); Ŋarra maypal bumara dhiyaku yothuwa (I got the shellfish for this child — bumara 'got' confirmed as printed (engine composes märraŋala — both valid takes)); Dhiyaku miyalkku märrma' yothu (This woman has two children); after the Lesson 47 verbs: Galkurru dhiyaku yolŋuwa (Wait for this man), Gurrupulu dhiyaku yolŋuwa (Give it to this man — dative recipient), Malthurru dhiyaku yolŋuwa (Go with this man). D. THIS = DHIYAŊU with -dhu/-thu/-yu/-y: Dhiyaŋu miyalkthu ŋanya nhäŋala (This woman saw him); Ŋarra yurru nhuna buma dhiyaŋu maŋal'yu (I'll hit you with this spearthrower). E. THIS = DHIYALA with -ŋura, ONLY when the verb is not in the present tense: Barpuru ŋayi ga nhina dhiyala bala'ŋura (Yesterday he was in this hut — barpuru + ga = the yesterday-continuous, user confirmed), Gäthura ŋayi gana nhinana dhiyala bala'ŋura, Goḏarr' ŋayi yurru nhini dhiyala bala'ŋura; NOTE: -mi (often with -ŋu-) is sometimes added: dhiyalaŋumi, same meaning. With a PRESENT tense verb or in verbless sentences dhuwala is used: Ŋayi ga nhina dhuwala bala'ŋura; Djamarkuḻi' dhuwala bala'ŋura (confirmed as printed: Djamarkuḻi' here, djamarrkuḻi' elsewhere).

F. THIS = DHIPALA with -lili: Rulwaŋdhurru dhipala tablelili (Put it on this table), Galkulu dhipala bathilili (Put it into this basket — user confirmed galkulu, the II of galkan 'put into'; the earlier Galkurru was a misread). G. THIS = DHIPUŊURU with -ŋuru: Dhipuŋuru ŋayi marrtjina wäŋaŋuru (He went from this place). H. THIS = DHIYAKALA with -gala/-kala/-wala: Gurrupulu dhiyakala miyalkkala (Give it to this woman), Nhini dhiyakala miyalkkala (Sit by this woman), Djuy'yurru dhiyakala miyalkkala (Send it with this woman). I. THIS = DHIYAKUŊU with -guŋu/-kuŋu/-wuŋu: Dhiyakuŋu miyalkkuŋu ŋarra dhäwu märraŋala (I got the story from this woman). J. THIS = DHIYAKALAŊUŊURU with -galaŋuŋuru: Yarrkthurru dhiyakalaŋuŋuru miyalkkalaŋuŋuru! (Move away from this girl!); note: one or both suffixes can be shortened (dhiyakala(ŋuŋuru) miyalkkala) as 'from' is in the verb. K. THIS = DHUWALAŊUWUY with -buy/-puy/-wuy: Ŋatha dhuwalaŋuwuy dharpapuy (The food is from this tree); Yolŋu dhuwalaŋuwuy wäŋapuy (The man is from this place). L. THIS = DHIYAKALAŊUWUY with -galaŋuwuy: Dhäwu ŋayi ŋarrakala ḻakaraŋala dhiyakalaŋuwuy yothuwalaŋuwuy (He told a story about this baby — ŋarrakala printed on the teller (confirmed)); NOTE: dhuwala yothunha can also be used. NOTES: 1. 'this' can stand without a noun: Dhiyaŋu ŋarranha bumara ŋayi (He hit me with this). 2. bala adds emphasis: Dhuwala bala yiki ŋarraku (This is my knife), Dhiyaku bala ŋarra djäl (I want this one). 3. suffix -dhi/-yi adds emphasis: Dhipuŋuruyi wäŋaŋuru ŋayi marrtjina (dealt with in a later Lesson). 4. word order is not fixed.

lessons.title: Where? / Here

rules.statement: A. Some of the words for 'this' are also used for 'here'. B. HERE = DHUWALA (stationary): verbless Dhuwala raki (Here is the rope — raki printed, engine raki'); with a present-tense verb Dhuwala ŋayi nhina ga (Here he is / sitting here), Djäma ŋayi ga dhuwala bala'ŋura (He is working here in the hut); Q Wanha Bäya? A Dhuwala. C. HERE = DHIYALA (stationary, when the person or thing is NOT present at this moment — verb not in present tense): Barpuru ŋayi ga dhiyala nhina (barpuru + ga = the yesterday-continuous — user confirmed, no anomaly), Gäthura ŋayi gana dhiyala nhinana, Goḏarr' ŋayi yurru dhiyala nhini, Dhiyala nhini! (Sit/stay here!); Q Wanha yiki? A Dhiyala gana ŋorrana (It was here, lit. lying); Q Wanhami/Wanhala ŋayi gana djäma? A Dhiyala; Q Nhe yurru wanhami/wanhala nhina? A Dhiyala. NOTE: -mi (often with -ŋu-) may be added: dhiyalaŋumi, same meaning. D. HERE = DHIPALA (movement towards): Gäŋu dhipala! (Bring it here!), Marrtji dhipala! (Come here!); Q Nhäkurru/Wanhawala/Nhälili ŋarra dhu nhirrpan? A Dhipala. NOTE: nhäkurru is not used at Yirrkala. E. HERE = DHIPUŊURU (movement away): Dhipuŋuru ŋayi marrtjina (He went from here); Q Wanhaŋuru? A Dhipuŋuru. F. HERE = DHUWALAŊUWUY (belonging): Ŋarraku miyalk dhuwalaŋuwuy (My wife belongs here); Q Wanhaŋuwuy nhe? A Dhuwalaŋuwuy. NOTES: 1. bala for emphasis (Dhuwala bala ŋayi ga nhina; Gäŋu dhipala bala). 2. suffix -dhi/-yi for emphasis (later Lesson). 3. word order is not fixed.

lessons.title: That

rules.statement: A. 'That' agrees with its noun by changing form completely, like 'this' (Lesson 54) — and has THREE series: dhuwali (visible, comparatively close), ŋunhi (also usable when not seen; frequently used where English says 'the', note 5), ŋunha (far). B base DHUWALI/ŊUNHI/ŊUNHA: Dhuwali guya ŋarraku; Dhuwali miyalk ŋorrana gana (was lying down); Ŋarra nhäŋala dhuwali miyalknha. C dative DHIYAKI/ŊURUKI/ŊURUKU (-gu/-ku/-wu/-wa): Ŋarra djäl/marŋgi yolŋuwa dhiyaki (I want/know that person); Guya ŋarra dharpuŋala dhiyaki miyalkku (I speared a fish for that woman); Dhiyaki yolŋuwa waŋgany yäna ḻuŋiny (That man has only one pipe); after the Lesson 47 verbs: Ŋayi wäthurruna/gitkitthurruna/gana djäka dhiyaki yothuwa. NOTE: ŋuruki is sometimes pronounced ŋuriki. D ergative/instrument DHIYAŊI/ŊURIŊI/ŊURUŊU (-dhu/-thu/-yu/-y): Dhiyaŋi wuŋgandhu ŋarranha ḻawuŋala (That dog bit me — wuŋgan; engine dog is waṯu with wuŋgan as base alterna; ḻawuŋala printed, engine ḻäwuma → ḻäwuŋala); Dhiyaŋi garay ŋarra bäru dharpuŋala (I speared the crocodile with that spear). NOTE: ŋuriŋi is sometimes pronounced ŋuruŋi. E -ŋura DHIYALI/ŊUNHILI/ŊUNHALA when NOT in that place now: Barpuru maṉḏa ga dhiyali dharpaŋura nhina (barpuru + ga = the yesterday-continuous — user confirmed, no anomaly), nhinana (today), nhini (tomorrow), Dhiyali dharpaŋura nhini (Sit by that tree); NOTE -mi/-ŋumi may be added (ŋunhiliŋumi/ŋunhilimi); AT THIS VERY MOMENT dhuwali/ŋunhi/ŋunha: Waṯu dhuwali dharpaŋura galki (near that tree); Miyalk dhuwali dharpaŋura dhärra ga (standing by that tree).

F -lili DHIPALI/ŊUNHIWILI/ŊUNHAWALA: Marrtji dhipali dhurrwaralili (Go to that door/gate). G -ŋuru DHIPUŊURU/ŊULIŊURU/ŊULAŊURU/BEŊURU/ŊUNHIŊURU: Ŋayi marrtjina dhipuŋuru wäŋaŋuru (He came from that place/camp/country). H -gala/-kala/-wala DHIYAKALA/ŊURIKALA/ŊURUKALA: Gurrupulu/Djuy'yurru/Nhini dhiyakala miyalkkala (Give it to / Send it with / Sit by that girl). I -guŋu/-kuŋu/-wuŋu DHIYAKUŊU/ŊURIKUŊU/ŊURUKUŊU: Ŋarra dhiyakuŋu miyalkkuŋu märraŋala dhäwu (I got the story from that woman). J -galaŋuŋuru DHIYAKALAŊUŊURU/ŊURIKALAŊUŊURU/ŊURUKALAŊUŊURU: Yarrkthurru dhiyakalaŋuŋuru yothuwalaŋuŋuru (Move away from that baby); NOTE: one or both suffixes may be shortened (dhiyakala yothuwala(ŋuŋuru), dhiyakala(ŋuŋuru) yothuwala). K -buy/-puy/-wuy DHUWALIŊUWUY/ŊUNHIŊUWUY/ŊUNHAŊUWUY: Dhuwala ŋatha dharpapuy dhuwaliŋuwuy (This food is from that tree). L -galaŋuwuy DHIYAKALAŊUWUY/ŊURIKALAŊUWUY/ŊURUKALAŊUWUY: Ŋayi dhäwu märraŋala dhiyakalaŋuwuy (He heard a story about that woman). NOTES: 1. 'that' can stand without a noun (Dhiyaŋi ŋarranha gurrupara — That person gave it to me). 2. bala for emphasis. 3. -dhi/-yi for emphasis (Ŋarra nhäŋala ŋunhiyi miyalknha). 4. the first word of each triple is for the visible and comparatively close; the others also serve when not seen. 5. ŋunhi is frequently used where English says 'the' (Barpuru ŋarra nhäma ŋunhi miyalknha). 6. some words for 'that' are the same as for 'this'.
