lessons.title: Completive aspect: bili

rules.statement: A. bili has many meanings; as a verb particle it denotes that the action HAS BEEN COMPLETED — translatable as 1. 'have' (I have washed), 2. 'have already', 3. emphasising the verb (I SAW it). Examples: a. Teacher: Gatjuy ḻupthurru(na)! — Child: Bili. (I have.) b. Wanha ŋarraku djurrany'tja? — BILI ŋarra nhuŋu gurrupara (I GAVE it to you / I've already given it to you). c. Nhaku nhe ŋanya dhirr'yurrunanydja? BILI ŋarra ŋunhi waŋananydja nhinanharawa mukthunarawa (Why did you wake him? I TOLD you to sit quietly). d. (news of a death) Dhiyaku bäpa bili dhiŋgaŋala (This person's father has died). e. Ŋathanydja ŋarranha gurrupuluna — Bäyŋuna dhuwala — BILI ŋarra nhäŋala ŋatha (I SAW some). f. Wanha Leku? — Bili marrtjinana ((He) has gone). g. Waŋi Stephennha marrtjinyarawa bäpawala — BILI ŋayi barpuru marrtji (He WENT yesterday). h. BILI ŋarra guyaŋana (I've remembered). i. BILI ŋarra maḻŋ'maraŋala (I've found it). NOTE: the L84 suffixes -na and -dja/-tja/-nydja/-ny'tja have been added in this Lesson (djurrany'tja, waŋananydja, marrtjinana, gurrupuluna, Bäyŋuna).

notes: Mechanism: FraseIR.bili — 'already' (EN, any position) / 'ya' (ES) stripped by extraerBili in the wrapper; the generar() tail prepends Bili to the finished clause (main + every alternativa), decapitalising the old first token unless it is the subject's proper name: 'i already gave it to you' → Bili ŋarra gurrupara nhokala (book b, with the nhuŋu dative among the alternativas); 'i already found it' → Bili ŋarra maḻŋ'maraŋala = example i letter-exact; 'he already went yesterday' → Bili barpuru ŋayi marrtji (book g order ŋayi-barpuru among alts)

lessons.title: Bitjan / nhaltjan

rules.statement: A. bitjan is an adverb with the four verb forms (compare mirithirri, L74): P bitjan, S biyaku, T bitjarra, Q bitjana(ra) — 'thus / like this / like that', AGREEING IN FORM with the verb it qualifies. Primary: Ŋayi barpuru bitjan waŋa (That's what he said yesterday); Walala ga bitjan nhina (They are sitting like this); Bitjan ŋayi ga wukirri. Secondary: Biyaku ḏar'ṯaryurru (Sing like this); Yaka biyaku waŋi (Don't talk like that); Ŋayi balaŋu biyaku guyaŋi (That's what he might think). Tertiary: Bitjarra ŋayi waŋana (That is what he said); Ŋarra bitjarra guyaŋana (That's what I thought); Walala gana bitjarra wukirri. Quaternary: Yaka ŋarra bitjana(ra) waŋanha(ra) (I didn't say that); Balaŋu ŋayi bitjana(ra) giritjinya(ra) (He should have danced like this); Yaka ŋarra marŋgi bitjanarawa ḏar'ṯaryunarawa (I don't know how to sing like that). NOTE: bitjan is often used without a verb — 'do' or 'say' understood: Yaka biyaku (Don't do that); Bitjarra ŋayi (That's what he said). B. nhaltjan is the interrogative of bitjan: P nhaltjan, S nhalayaku, T nhaltjarra, Q nhaltjana(ra) — 'how', 'why' or 'what', agreeing with the verb: Nhaltjan nhe ga guyaŋa(nydja)? (What do you think?); Nhaltjan ŋarra dhu wukirri(nydja)? (What/How shall I write?); Nhaltjan nhe ga ŋäthi(nydja)? (Why are you crying?); Nhalayaku ŋayi balaŋu guyaŋi(nydja)? (What might he think?); Nhaltjarra ŋayi gana giritjina(nydja)? (How was he dancing?); Nhaltjarra maṉḏa waŋana(nydja)? (What did they say?). NOTES: 1. without a verb, 'say/do' understood: Nhaltjan? (Pardon?); Nhaltjan nhe ga? (What are you doing?); Nhaltjan(na) limurru dhu? (What shall we do?); Nhaltjarra walala? 2. not always interrogative: Nhaltjan ŋarra dhu waŋa(nydja)? (What shall I say?); Nhaltjanarawa nhe djälnydja waŋanharawa (Whatever you want to say — nhaltjanarawa because of djäl). 3. bracketed -na and -dja/-tja/-nydja/-ny'tja may be omitted; -nydja is very common at the end of a question, especially one ending in a verb.

notes: bitjan COMPOSES as pure data: a verbs.json entry (I bitjan, II biyaku, III bitjarra, IV bitjana/bitjanara) + MANERAS entries ('like this/like that/thus', ES 'así') — the L74 aplicarManera machinery then handles the FORM AGREEMENT automatically: Yaka waŋi biyaku! (fronted Yaka biyaku waŋi! = the book's S2 among alts), Ḏar'ṯaryurru biyaku!/Biyaku ḏar'ṯaryurru! = S1, Walala ga (bitjan) nhina = P2

nhaltjan COMPOSES as a new interrogative frame: EN [what|how|why]+[do/does|are/is/am|did|was/were|shall/will]+PRON+V and ES [qué|cómo|por qué]+preterite → predicado {interrogativo, clave nhaltjan, estado verbo}; the generator picks the AGREEING nhaltjan form from verbs.json (I nhaltjan+ga/dhu, III nhaltjarra(+gana)) and offers the verb+nydja alternativa via the NEW sufijoNydja helper — the L84-B sandhi table finally as code (nasals→dja, stops/nasal-glottal→tja, vowels/liquids/y/w→nydja, plain glottal→ny'+tja): Nhaltjan nhe ga guyaŋa(nydja)? = B1 letter-exact incl. the bracketed suffix

lessons.title: Dhuwalatjan / ŋula(wi)tjan / wanha(wi)tjan: this way, that way, which way

rules.statement: A. In L54/56 'this' and 'that' behave as adjectives agreeing with their nouns. B. With nouns ending in the perlative -gurru/-kurru/-wurru, the words dhuwalatjan and ŋulatjan are used instead — they behave as ADVERBS qualifying the VERB, conjugated like bitjan/nhaltjan (L86). PRIMARY: Barpuru ŋayi dhuwalatjan/ŋula(wi)tjan marrtji dhukarrkurru (Yesterday he walked along this/that path); Walala ga marrtji dhuwalatjan/ŋula(wi)tjan wäŋakurru (They are going through this country); Ŋarranydja yurru dhuwalatjan/ŋula(wi)tjan waṉḏirri dhawaḏakurru (I'll run along this/that beach). SECONDARY: Marrtji dhuwalayaku/ŋulayaku dhukarrkurru (Go along this/that path). TERTIARY: Bäpi djuryurruna dhuwalatjarra/ŋula(wi)tjarra dharpakurru (The snake crawled over this/that log). QUATERNARY: Balaŋu ŋayi marrtjinya(ra) dhuwalatjana(ra)/ŋula(wi)tjana(ra) dhukarrkurru (He should have gone along this/that path). C. wanha(wi)tjan is the interrogative, same conjugation: Wanha(wi)tjan ŋayi yurru dhukarrkurru marrtjinydja? (Along which path will he go?); Nhumanydja yurru wanha(wi)yaku dhukarrkurru marrtjinydja?; Wanha(wi)tjarra ŋayi dhukarrkurru marrtjinanydja? (…did he go?); Walala balaŋu wanha(wi)tjana dhukarrkurru marrtjinya(ra)nydja? (…should they have gone?). D. Also without a -kurru noun: Wanha(wi)tjan limurru dhu? (Which way shall we go?) — answers: Dhuwalatjan bala / Bitjan bala / Ŋulatjan bala (This/that way); Dhuwalayaku bala marrtji / Biyaku bala marrtji / Ŋulayaku bala marrtji (Go this/that way). NOTES: 1. bala is not essential but very common (emphasis). 2. bitjan (biyaku etc.) is often used in this sense. 3. bracketed (wi) may be omitted: Ŋulatjarra/Ŋulawitjarra ŋayi marrtjina. 4. wanhaŋuwurru is sometimes used instead of wanhawitjan. 5. -nydja may be omitted but is very common on the verb at the end of a question.

lessons.title: Balanya(ra): thus, like this, like that

rules.statement: A. balanya(ra) is the counterpart of bitjan: bitjan (thus/like this/like that) is an ADVERB qualifying verbs (L86); balanya(ra) is an ADJECTIVE qualifying nouns: Balanya(ra) nhanŋu rom (That is what his way of life is like); Ŋarraku djoŋgu balanya(ra) (This is what my hat is like); Balanya(ra) nhanukuŋu wukirriwuynydja (This is what his writing is like); Balanya(ra) ŋunhi miyalktja (That's the sort of woman she is). Q: Nhäthinya(ra) djakany'tja? (What size/How tall?) — A: Balanya(ra) (indicating with hand); Q: Nhäthinya(ra) miny'tjinydja? (What colour?) — A: Balanya(ra). NOTES: 1. balanyara is used at Yirrkala instead of balanya. 2. balanyara sometimes at Elcho and Milingimbi, balanya more common — same meaning. B. Suffixes on balanya(ra): 1. + -ŋuru: Walala gana yay'yayurruna mirithina. Balanyaŋuru ŋayi walalanha ŋarrtjurrunanydja (They were making a lot of noise. That's why — lit. from that — he told them off). 2. + -mirriy (L81): Nhätha ŋayi dhiŋgaŋalanydja? Balanyamirriy Mr Ellemor gana nhinana dhiyala (When did he die? At the time Mr Ellemor was here). 3. balanyara + -gu/-ku/-wa/-wu: Ŋarra balanyarawa djäl dressku (I want a dress like this); Balanyarawadhi ŋarra marrtjinanydja (That's why I came — purpose). 4. balanyara + -dhu/-thu/-yu/-y: Dharrwamirri nhuma ŋuli bunhamirrinydja balanyaray nyal'yu dhäwuy (You often fight because of untrue stories such as that); Balanyaraydhi ŋayi gäthura rirrikthurrunanydja (That's why she was sick today). NOTE: balanya is much wider than bitjan — it refers to FACTS expressible as whole sentences ('The children stole money and then lied about it. That's why — balanyaŋuru — he spoke angrily to them'). C. Comparisons use nhakuna 'like' with balanya: Ŋarraku yiki balanya nhakuna nhuŋu (My knife is like yours); Dhuwala mitjiyaŋ balanya nhakuna Ḻarrpan (This boat is like the Ḻarrpan); Nhanŋu djurra' ḏarrtjalk balanya nhakuna dhuwala (His book is clean like this one). NOTES: 1. often yäna is added — nearest English 'just': Dhuwalanydja mitjiyaŋ yindi nhakuna Ḻarrpan yäna. 2. the L84 suffixes have been added. 3. nhakuna can be used without balanya.

(C) comparisons: FraseIR.comparado — 'X is (ADJ) like Y' in the possessive-subject and demonstrative-subject copula frames (ES 'es como') → [adjective|balanya] nhakuna [término] with the yäna alternativa (note 1): Ŋarraku yiki balanya nhakuna nhuŋu = C1 letter-exact, Nhanŋu djorra' ḏarrtjalk balanya nhakuna dhuwala = C3 letter-exact; comparison terms cover possessive pronouns (yours/el tuyo), names, nouns and 'this one'. (B1/B3) FraseIR.balanyaNuru — sentence-initial "that's why" / 'por eso' prepends Balanyaŋuru with the Balanyarawadhi purpose form (B3) as alternativa: Balanyaŋuru ŋarra marrtjina. BONUS frame: possessive-subject + copula + plain adjective now composes at all ('my knife is big' → Ŋarraku yiki yindi was null) and the verbless subject render finally emits sujeto.posesivo

lessons.title: Bili meaning only / just / same

rules.statement: A. bili has many uses; here it denotes 'only', 'just' or 'same'. B. THIS/THAT + BILI (L54/56): 1. DHUWALA BILI: Dhuwala(na) bili ŋarraku yothunydja (He is my only child — lit. this only my child); Yaka. Dhuwala bili (No, this will do — this only). 2. DHUWALI BILI: Yaka. Dhuwali(na) bili (No, that's all / it's the same one). 3. ŊUNHI BILI: Yaka dhu wiripu mala marrtji — ŋunhi bili djarr'yunawuy yäna (The others are not to go — just the chosen ones only). 4. DHIYAKU BILI: Yaka. Dhiyaku bili ŋarra djälnydja (No, I just want this one). 5. ŊURUKI BILI: Ŋurukidhi bili (His too — that same person's). 6. DHIYALA BILI: Yaka. Dhiyala bili ŋarra gana djäma (I've only been working here). 7. ŊUNHILI BILI: Ga ŋunhilidhi bili ŋayi yurru nhinanydja (He'll stay in the same place — there only). 8. ŊUNHIWILI BILI: Ŋunhiwilidhi/Ŋunhawalayi bili ((I'm going) there too — to there only, the same place). 9. DHIYAŊU BILI: a. time — Nhätha walala marrtjina? Dhiyaŋu bili (Just now); b. instrument — Yaka. Dhiyaŋu bili (Just this one — with this only). 10. ŊURUŊI BILI: a. time — Ŋuruŋiyi bili waluy ŋayi dhiŋgaŋalanydja (On that same day he died); b. agent — Ŋuruŋidhi bili (She did — that same person). C. BALANYA + BILI (L88): Nhanŋu Bäpa ḻiya-ḏäl ga ŋayinydja balanyayi bili (His father is clever and he is the same); Maṉḏa ŋunhi balanya bili djaka' (They are the same size); Mitjiyaŋ ga garrwarpuy yurru buna balanyaraydhi bili waluy (The boat and plane will arrive on the same day). D. BITJAN + BILI (L86, agreeing in form): 1. TIME (every day / all the time): P Ŋayinydja ŋuli ga bitjan bili rirrikthun yäna (He is sick all the time); S Biyaku bili nhini galki ŋarrakala (Stay near me all the time); T Ŋayi gana bitjarra bili gitkitthurruna yäna (He kept on laughing all the time); Q Ŋäthili ŋayi ŋuli ganha bitjana(ra) bili buḻ'yuna(ra) (He used to be always playing before). 2. 'thus only / just like / the same': P Ŋayi ga mari djäma bitjandhi bili nhakuna walala (He is making trouble just like they do); S Nhuma ŋuli mukthurru nhini biyakudhi bili nhakuna barpuru (Sit quietly just like yesterday); T Bäpa nhanŋu burakina ga ŋayinydja bitjarrayi bili (His father got hurt and he did the same); Q Nhe balaŋu bitjana(ra)yi bili waŋanha(ra) (You should have said the same). NOTES: 1. yäna is optional but very common. 2. the L84 suffixes are used throughout.

lessons.title: Asking questions

rules.statement: A. INTONATION: intonation plays a large part; by the rise in pitch we indicate an answer is expected. English also reverses word order (He has washed himself / Has he washed himself?). In Gupapuyŋu word order gives NO indication — often intonation alone is relied on: Nhe yurru buḻ'yun. (You will play) vs Nhe yurru buḻ'yun? (Will you play?). B. MUKA PLUS INTONATION — added to a question it is similar to English tags 'isn't it'/'didn't you': 1. Nhenydja ŋatha märraŋala muka? (You got the food, didn't you?); 2. Buḻ'yun ŋayi ga muka? (He's playing isn't he?); 3. Muka Darwinlili ŋayi marrtjina? (He went to Darwin, didn't he?). NOTES: 1. muka in itself is not a question indicator — intonation indicates the question; with a statement muka seems to denote emphasis. 2. muka questions can also be translated plain: Buḻ'yun ŋayi ga muka? = Is he playing?. C. BILI PLUS INTONATION — English 'Did you...(do something)?' / 'Has he...(done something)?' can often be translated using bili: 1. Bili nhe märraŋala? (Did you get (it)? / Have you got (it)?); 2. Bili ŋayi ḻupthurruna? (Has he washed?); 3. Bili maṉḏa nhäŋala? (Did/Have they (two) see(n) (it)?); 4. Bili nhuma ŋäkula? (Did/Have you hear(d)?); 5. Bili walala marrtjina? (Did/Have they go(ne)?); 6. Bili nhe ḻukana? (Did/Have you eat(en) (it)?); 7. Bili ŋayi dhiŋgaŋala? (Did/Has she die(d)?). NOTE: bili in itself is not a question indicator — intonation indicates the question. D. WANHA AS QUESTION INDICATOR — wanha (not asking 'where') can be used as a question or request indicator. Wanha plus SECONDARY form of verb: 1. Wanha nhe (balaŋu/ŋuli) ŋanya guŋga'yurrunydja?; 2. Wanha nhe (balaŋu/ŋuli) ŋanya gurrupulunydja?; 3. Wanha nhe (balaŋu/ŋuli) ŋanya marŋgikuŋunydja?; 4. Wanha nhe (balaŋu/ŋuli) ŋanya ŋäṉ'thurrunydja? — each glossed 'Will you / Why don't you / What about / How about' + help him / give (it) to him / teach him / ask him. Wanha plus QUATERNARY form: Wanha nhe (balaŋu/ŋuli) märranha(ra)nydja? / nhänha(ra)nydja? / ŋänha(ra)nydja? / gänha(ra)nydja? / ḻupthuna(ra)nydja? = Why did/didn't you get/see/hear/bring it / have a wash?. NOTES: 1. balaŋu or ŋuli can be included or omitted. 2. Context and tone of voice indicate whether the question means 'Did you?' or 'Why didn't you?'. 3. wanha can be a question indicator in a VERBLESS sentence: Wanha ŋatha dharrwa ŋunhi? (Is there plenty of food over there?). E. INTERROGATIVE WORDS — many words are themselves questions, even used alone: 1. Nhä (and suffixes): Nhä ŋunhanydja? (What's that?), Nhä walala dhäwunydja märraŋala? (What news did they get?), Nhaku (nhäku) nhe djälnydja? (15), Nhaku ŋayi ga ŋäthinydja? (31), Bäyanydja nhaku räli marrtjina? (31), Nhaliy nhe ŋanya bumaranydja? (33), Nhaliy ŋayi rirrikthurrunanydja? (66), Nhaliy waluy dhu mitjiyaŋdja dhiyala? (81), Nhälili ŋarra yurru galkandja? (27), Nhäŋuru maṉḏa ga bunhamirrinydja? (82), Nhäpuy dhuwalanydja? (39), Nhäkurru (wanhawala) nhe ga dhuwala marrtjinydja? (27). 2. Nhämirri: Nhämirri nhenydja? (How are you?), Nhämirri dhuwalanydja yolŋu — rerrimirri? (What's wrong with this person — is he sick?), Nhämirri ŋarranydja? (What about me?), Nhämirri balaŋu nhe ŋarranha guŋga'yurrunydja? (What/How about (you) helping me?), Ga nhämirri nhenydja rraku dhurrparama djurra' barpuru? (And what about (the fact that) you trod on mine yesterday?). 3. Nhätha: Nhätha dhu mitjiyaŋdja dhiyala? (When will the boat be here?), Nhätha ŋayi dhawal-guyaŋananydja? (When was he born?). 4. Nhäthinya(ra): Nhäthinya(ra) nhuŋu dresstja? (What's your dress like?), miny'tjinydja? (colour), djakany'tja? (size/height/length), gorrnydja? (width), goḏunydja? (distance by water), Nhäthinya(ra) ŋayi ŋathanydja gurrupara? (How much food did he give? — Answer: Dharrwa / Ḻurrkun' (only a little)). 5. Nhämunha': Nhämunha' ga ŋorranydja? (How many are there — lying?), Nhämunha' ga yolŋu giritjirrinydja? (How many people are dancing?), Nhuŋunydja dhuwali nhämunha' gulaka? (32), Nhämunharay' guyanydja barrtjurruna? (22), Nhämunha'mirri ŋayi nhuna ŋäṉ'thurrunanydja? (40), Nhämunha'mirri balanya Darwindja? (How much is one like that in Darwin?). NOTE: glottal stop at end of nhämunha' is optional; it must be inserted in nhämunha'mirri. 6. Nhaltjan (L86): Nhaltjan nhe dhu? (What will you do?), Nhaltjarra ŋayi waŋana? (What did he say?), Nhaltjarra nhe moŋala? (Why did you forget?), Nhaltjan ŋarra dhu djäma? (How shall I do (it)?). 7. Yol (and suffixes): Yol marrtjinanydja? (24), Yolthu ḻukananydja? (22/23), Yolnha ŋayi nhäŋalanydja? (19/20), Yolku dhuwalanydja? (13), Yolkuŋu dhuwalanydja? (30), Yolkala nhe ga nhinanydja? (26), Yolkalaŋuwuy nhuma gana waŋanhaminanydja? (39). 8. Wanha (and suffixes): Wanha yikinydja? (55/57), Wanhami gana ŋorrananydja? (55/57), Wanhala nhe yurru marrtjinydja?, Wanhaŋuwa nhe djäl nhinanharawanydja? (44), Wanhaŋuru nhenydja? (28), Wanhaŋuwuy nhenydja? (39), Wanhawitjan nhuma yurru marrtjinydja? (87). NOTES: 1. bracketed numbers refer to lessons. 2. in conversation these interrogative words are often used by themselves. 3. the suffix -dja/-tja/-nydja/-ny'tja (L84) occurs many times in this lesson — it often appears in questions, especially attached to a sentence-final verb, and may also be omitted.

He went to Darwin, didn't he?

lessons.title: Yanapi

rules.statement: A. yanapi often conveys 'I (he/she/etcetera) thought ... but was mistaken.' It is used with SECONDARY or QUATERNARY verb forms: 1. Yanapi ŋarraku. (I/he/she/they thought it was mine — but it isn't); 2. Yanapi ŋäṉḏi'mirriŋu. (She thought it was her mother — but she was mistaken); 3. Yanapi walala barpuru bili dharpuŋu gatapaŋa. (I thought they speared the buffalo yesterday — but I was mistaken); 4. Yanapi maṉḏa waṉḏinya(ra). (I thought they had run away — but they haven't). NOTE: the verb guyaŋa may be used as well, e.g. SUBJ-nydja ŋunhi guyaŋa yanapi ŋunhi ... (We thought he was a ... — religious example omitted by request). B. yanapi with a QUESTION infers the speaker has heard something which may or may not be correct: 1. Yapa, yanapi dhu djamarrkuḻi' yuwalk Darwinlili marrtji? (Sister, is it true that the children are going to Darwin?); 2. Nhä dhuwalanydja yuwalk yanapi dhu Goŋay' ga Djapala märranhamirri? (Is it true that Goŋay' and Djapala are getting married?); 3. Wäwa, nhä dhuwalanydja... yuwalk, yanapi Mr Symons dhu buna? (Wäwa, is it true that Mr Symons is coming?); 4. Yanapi ŋayi yaka djäl djämawa? (Is it true that he doesn't want work?); 5. Yuwalk yanapi ŋuruŋi miyalkthu ŋuli gi munatha ḻuki? (Is it true that that woman eats dirt?). NOTE: when dhu or yurru (future) are used, the Primary (Same-Day Future, L11) or Secondary (Tomorrow Future, L7) forms of the verb are used.

lessons.title: Interjections which lend emphasis to verbs

rules.statement: A. ḏutj is an interjection carrying the meaning of roŋiyirri/return; with the verb it gives emphasis: Marrtjina ŋayi dhakallili ga ḏutj roŋiyina. (He went to the island and then came back.) It can be used WITHOUT the verb, still carrying its meaning, and its form never changes (no primary/secondary etc forms): Marrtjina ŋayi ḏiltjilili ga ḏutj. (He went to the bush and came back again.) B. Gupapuyŋu has a number of these interjections, each associated with a particular verb: nhäma/see → dharr; wutthun/hit, shoot → ḏal (contrast ḏäl/strong); dhiŋgama/die, faint → ḏay; roŋiyirri/return → ḏutj or ḏitj (contrast ḏetj/grasshopper); ŋorra/sleep, lie down → buḻarr or ḏuy (contrast ḏoy'/money); ganan/ganarrthama/leave → bay'; ŋurrkama/throw away → bat; ŋayathama/hold → baṯ; dhärra/stand → birr; nhirrpan/put → djip; dhärra/stand → djip; dharpuma/spear → djat or giṯ; nhina/sit → dhut; gurrupan/give → gurray; marrtji/go → ḻarr'; ḻaw'yun/get up and go → ḻarr'. C. Frequently the suffix -nha is added to these interjections (L84 C; it may be omitted — meaning remains the same): 1. Ḻarr'nha walala, ḏutjnha walala, nhinana wäŋiya Miliŋinbi. (Off they went, then back they came and sat down at Milingimbi.); 2. Barpuru ŋayi ŋatha gäma wäŋalili, gurraynha gurrupan walalanha. (Yesterday she took food to the camp and gave it to them.); 3. Dharrnha nhäŋuna! (Look!); 4. Djipnha nhirrpulu! (Put (it) down!); 5. Guya ŋayi nhäŋala giṯnha dharpuŋala. (He saw the fish and speared it.); 6. Baṯ! (or Baṯnha!) (Hold (it)!); 7. Dhuŋgur'yurruna ŋayi, bay'nha. (He set fire to it, then left.); 8. Ḏuynha ŋorrina! (Go to sleep! (Lie down!)). NOTE: suffix -na (L84) has been added to some commands.

lessons.title: Joining clauses together — ga/bala/bili/ŋanydja/yurru (conjunctions)

rules.statement: A. Up till now sentences have contained only one clause; two or more clauses in one sentence are joined in various ways. B. GA/and: Yothunydja ḻupthurruna gäthura ga waŋganydja miyalk waṉḏinana ga ḻaw'maraŋala ŋanya ŋunhi ga Yapawalana gäŋala hospitallili. (A child nearly drowned today and a woman ran and picked him (lit. him that one) up and took him to the hospital to Sister.) NOTES: 1. many sentences begin with ga; 2. sometimes ga has no English equivalent and is used for emphasis only: Ga miyalkthunydja ŋunhi dharrwaynydja ga nhäŋalana ŋanya. (And lots of women saw him.) C. BALA/and, then, so — used the same way as ga: 1. Ŋayi yurru märrama djoŋgu bala nhirrpanna ḻiyalilina. (He'll get a hat and put it on his head.); 2-3. (religious examples omitted by request). D. BILI/and, then, so: Ŋarra gana nhinana ga Boŋa, bili gana ŋatha ŋorrana bala'ŋura bili Boŋanydja mirithina djaŋŋarrthina bili ŋayi gana ḻukana ŋatha. (Boŋa and I were sitting down and some food was in the house and Boŋa was very hungry so she ate the food.) E. ŊANYDJA/or: 1. Walala bili buḏapthurruna ŋanydja dhuwala bandji walala ga nhina? (Have they gone across or are they still here?); 2. Dhuwalanydja nhuŋu ŋanydja ŋarraku? (Is this yours or mine?). NOTE — when 'or' joins two WORDS (not clauses): (a) maku, (b) nhä maku, (c) yol maku, (d) wanha maku: 1. Märrma' maku ḻurrkun yurru marrtji. (Two or three will go.); 2. Ŋarra dhu yiki märrama nhä maku djalwarra. (I'll get a knife or some trousers.); 3. Boŋa yurru marrtji yol maku Ḻorru. (Boŋa or Lorru will go.); 4. Ŋayi ga nhina Ḏalmana wanha maku Ḏirrpu'ŋura. (He is at Ḏalmana or Howard Island.) F. ŊANYDJA or YURRU/but — both mean 'but'. If the previous clause is NEGATIVE or contains yanapi or balaŋu (might, should have etc), the second clause is joined by ŊANYDJA: 1. Mitjiyaŋ yaka dhiyala bunanhara ŋanydja djulkthurruna bala Darwinlili. (The boat didn't call here, but went on to Darwin.); 2. Balaŋu ŋayi ŋäŋ'thunara, ŋanydja bäyŋu warray. (He should have asked, but he didn't.); 3. Balaŋu ŋayi roŋiyinyara, ŋanydja muŋbunuŋalana ŋayi marrtjinanydja. (He should have come back, but went for good.); 4. Yanapi ŋayi bili mänŋu (user confirmed — short secondary of märrama), ŋanydja bäyŋu warray. (They thought he had got it, but he hadn't — see L91.) NOTE: warray has no English equivalent. If the previous clause is POSITIVE and does not contain yanapi or balaŋu, the second clause is joined by YURRU: 1. (religious example omitted by request); 2. Ŋarranydja ŋuli ga bitjan bili waŋa yäna walalanha, yurru walalanydja ŋuli gi yakana märr-yuwalkthi. (I tell them every day but they don't take any notice.); 3. Ŋarranydja djäl dhiyaki yikiwa, yurru bäyŋu ŋarraku rrupiyanydja. (I want that knife, but I haven't any money.) G. Sometimes clauses are put side by side with NO joining word: Waṉḏina ŋayi, storelili gärrina, mel-ḻaŋ'ḻaŋdhurruna ŋarali'wa. (He ran, entered the store and looked around for tobacco.) (From a story; an isolated sentence would probably use connecting words.)

lessons.title: Dependent clauses (1) introduced by ŋunhi (that/which/what/who)

rules.statement: A. ŋunhi very often joins two clauses; it translates 'that', 'which', 'who' or 'what'. B. ŊUNHI/that (complement clauses): 1. Ŋarranydja dhäwu ŋäkula gäthura ŋunhi maṉḏa barpuru waṉḏirri. (I heard that they ran away today.); 2. Ŋarranydja marŋgi ŋunhi nhe ŋuli ga bitjan bili djäma yäna. (I know that you work every day.); 3. Bäpay ŋarraku ḻakaraŋala ŋunhi dhu mitjiyaŋdja yalala buna. (Bäpa told me that the boat would arrive later.); 4. (religious example omitted by request); 5. Linyu nhuna dhu yaka ḻakarama ŋunhi nhe gana ŋatha manaŋina. (We won't tell on you for stealing the food — lit. that you stole the food.) C. ŊUNHI/which, what: 1. Dhiyaki ŋarra djälnydja ŋunhi ŋorra ga galki bala'ŋura. (I want that one which is lying near the hut.); 2. Bili ŋayi maḻŋ'maraŋala yiki ŋunhi ŋarra gana ḻarruŋala gäthura. (He has found the knife which I was looking for today.); 3. Moŋalana ŋarra ŋunhiyinydja ŋunhi barpuru ŋali ga ŋarrtjunmirri. (I have forgotten what — lit. that which — we were arguing about yesterday.); 4. Wanha rrupiya ŋunhi barpuru nhe manaŋirri? (Where's the money which you stole yesterday?); 5. Ŋarranydja yurru dhäwu ḻakarama ŋunhiŋuwuy ŋunhi gäthura ŋali gana wukirri. (I'll tell (you) something about what — lit. about that which — we were writing today.) D. ŊUNHI PLUS PERSONAL PRONOUN = who: 1. (religious example omitted by request); 2. Ŋunhiwurruna bili walŋanydja, ŋunhi walala gana mitjiyaŋŋura guḻŋi'kulŋiyina. (Only those who were in the ship were alive.); 3. Ŋarra dhägir'yurruna djamarrkuḻi'nha ŋunhi barpuru walala ŋatha manaŋirri. (I punished the children who stole the food yesterday.); 4. Ŋarra nhäŋala ŋunhiyi yolŋunha ŋunhi Djäway nhanŋu rrupiya gurrupan. (I saw the person to whom Djäwa gave money.); 5. Napurrunydja maḻŋ'maraŋalana ŋunhiyi miyalknha ŋunhi nhuma gana gäthura nhanŋu ḻarruŋala. (We found the woman for whom you were looking today.); 6. Gäthura ŋayi bunananydja ŋarraku ŋunhinydja ŋunhi nhuma barpuru ŋanya nhäma. (Today he — that one — whom you saw yesterday came to me.) NOTE: sometimes yol (yolthu/yolnha/yolku etc) is used instead of or in addition to the pronoun: Ŋarra dhägir'yurruna djamarrkuḻi'nha ŋunhi yolthu walala gana ŋatha manaŋina; Ŋarra nhäŋala ŋunhiyi yolŋunha yolku ŋunhi Djäway rrupiya gurrupan. E. Sometimes such clauses are put together with NO connecting words: 1. Marŋgi nhuma ŋarraku Bäpa dhiyala dhiŋgaŋala. (You know my father died here.); 2. Wanhana ŋaraliny'tja barpuru nhe manaŋirri? (Where's the tobacco you stole yesterday?); 3. Ŋunhana ŋunhi yolŋunydja walala, gäthura ŋali gana ḻarrunala walalaŋgu. (There are the people we were looking for today.)

lessons.title: Dependent clauses (2) introduced by ŋunhi/ŋuli/bäy (when)

rules.statement: A. ŋunhi, ŋuli or bäy introduce a clause denoting time (when): 1. Ŋarraku wäthurru ŋunhi/ŋuli/bäy dhu gapunydja buŋbuŋdhun. (Call me when the water boils.); 2. Ŋarra dhu nhuna gurrupulunydja ŋunhi/ŋuli/bäy dhu mitjiyaŋ buni. (I'll give it to you when the boat comes — buni tomorrow-future, L7.); 3. Ŋayi dhu nhokala galkithirrina ŋunhi/ŋuli/bäy dhu walu gilitjirri dhiŋganharawa. (He'll be near you when the time comes (approaches) to die.); 4. Napurrunydja ŋuli djämalilina marrtji ŋunhi/ŋuli/bäy bellnydja ŋuli wutthun. (We go to work when the bell rings — L62.); 5. (religious example omitted by request). B. The temporal clause may PRECEDE the principal: 1. Ŋunhi/ŋuli/bäy napurru marrtjina guyalili (ga) napurru nhäŋala yawirriny'nha. (When we went fishing we saw the single boys.); 2. Ŋunhi/ŋuli/bäy dhu Bäpanydja buna, (ga) ŋarranydja yurru ŋanya ŋäŋ'thunna rrupiyawana. (When Bäpa comes I'll ask him for money.) NOTES: 1. Gupapuyŋu says 'Call me when the water WILL boil' — in temporal clauses English uses present tense for future happenings; 2. when the temporal clause precedes the principal, a connecting word such as ga or bala is sometimes used: Ŋunhi dhu bell wutthun (ga) napurru dhu marrtji djämalilina. (When the bell goes, we'll go to work.)

lessons.title: Dependent clauses (3) introduced by ŋuli/ŋunhi/balaŋu (if)

rules.statement: A. A conditional (if) clause may be introduced by any of: ŋuli / ŋunhi / balaŋu / ŋuli balaŋu / ŋunhi balaŋu. B. When the conditional refers to a PROBABLE FUTURE action, either construction: 1. dhu or yurru + PRIMARY verb form: Ŋuli (etc) yurru ŋayi miyalknhanydja djaw'yun ŋayinydja ŋuli balaŋu yurru mari märrama yindina. (If he runs away with a woman he'll get into a lot of trouble.); 2. SECONDARY form: Ŋuli (etc) ŋayi miyalknhanydja djaw'yurru, ŋayinydja balaŋu mari mänŋu (user confirmed — the short secondary of märrama, listed in the verb table; the print can read mäŋŋu) yindina. (If he runs away with a woman he might get into a lot of trouble.) C. When the conditional refers to a probable action in the PAST, the QUATERNARY form is used: Ŋuli (etc) ŋayi miyalknhanydja djaw'yuna(ra), ŋayinydja balaŋu mari märranha(ra) yindina. (If he had run away with a woman, he would/might have got into a lot of trouble.) D. More examples: 1. Ŋuli dhu nhe bulu bitjan ga napurrunydja dhu nhuna dhägir'yunna. (If you do that again, we'll punish you.); 2. Ŋunhi ŋayi balaŋu biyaku walalanha ŋarrtjurru, ga walalanydja balaŋu ŋanya buŋuna. (If he tells them off like that, they might hit him.); 3. Balaŋu ŋayi djälthinya(ra) ŋayinydja balaŋu marrtjinya(ra) warray. (If he had wanted to, he could have gone.) NOTES: 1. when the main clause follows the conditional it may be joined by a connecting word (e.g. ga) — not essential; 2. warray has no real equivalent in English.

lessons.title: Dependent clauses (4) introduced by wanha balaŋu (whether)

rules.statement: A dependent clause introduced by wanha balaŋu translates 'whether' or 'if'. Wanha balaŋu is ALWAYS followed by the secondary or quaternary form of the verb (except in verbless sentences — examples 2 and 3): 1. Guya dhuwali nhära ga — mänŋu (user re-checked p164: mänŋu, the short secondary of märrama already in the verb table) wanha balaŋu borumdhinya(ra). (There's a fish cooking there — get it (and see) whether/if it is done — lit. if it has become cooked.); 2. Waṉḏi ga wapthurru wanha balaŋu nhe rurrkrurrk wapthunarawa. (Run and jump (to see) whether/if you are light (enough) for jumping.); 3. Mitjiyaŋ walala bili nhäŋala. Maku nhäŋu wanha balaŋu galki nhä maku baḏak barrku yäna. (They've seen the boat. Just have a look (and see) whether/if it's close or still far off.); 4. Yolŋu ŋunha rirrikthun ga wäŋiya. Maku marrtji ga nhäŋu ŋanya wanha balaŋu ŋayi gi rirrikthurru baḏak. (There's a person sick in the camp. Just go and have a look at him (to see) whether/if he is still sick.) NOTES: 1. nhära is intransitive (cook/burn), bathan is transitive (cook/burn); 2. maku with a command can usually be translated 'just'; 3. nhä maku = or; 4. yäna has no English equivalent; 5. baḏak means 'still'; 6. English usually needs to insert 'and see'/'to see' — Gupapuyŋu has no equivalent; 7. sometimes a clause introduced by ŋuli is best translated 'whether': Ŋuli nhe dhu bilyun manymaklili ga nhä maku yätjkurrulili nhuŋuwuy mala-djarr'yunarawa. (Whether you turn to the good (way) or to the bad is for you to decide.)

lessons.title: Dependent clauses (5) introduced by bili (because)

rules.statement: A. Often bili joins two clauses where English says 'because': 1. Walala djulŋithinana bili mitjiyaŋ yurru yalala buna. (They are happy because the boat will arrive later on.); 2. Ŋayi balaŋu ŋarranha ŋarrtjurru bili yaka ŋayi djäl balanyarawa romgu. (He might tell me off because he doesn't like that sort of thing.); 3. Ŋarranydja dhuwala ga rirrikthun bili barpuru ŋarra guya ḻuka ḏulki. (I am sick because I ate a bad fish yesterday.); 4. Yothu ga ŋäthi bili ŋuruŋi miyalkthu ŋanya ŋathanydja gombuŋala. (The baby is crying because that woman took his food from him.); 5. Wäway ŋarranha wutthurruna bili ŋarra ŋanya matha gurrupara yätjkurru. (Wäwa hit me because I swore at him — lit. gave him bad language.)

lessons.title: Dependent clauses (6) introduced by märr (ga) (because/(so) that)

rules.statement: A dependent clause introduced by märr (ga) translates 'because', 'so that' or 'that'. MÄRR (GA)/SO THAT, THAT: 1-2. (religious examples omitted by request); 3. Dhiyala nhini märr (ga) nhe yurru yaka ŋanya warku'yun. (Sit here (so) that you won't annoy him.); 4. Nhämirri dhuwalanydja - marimirri? - märr (ga) ŋayi dhuwala dhakatjurruna. (What's wrong with this (person) — is he angry (about something) that he is looking so sullen. dhakatjun = have sulky, morose expression of face.); 5. Balaŋu nhe gurrupanara märr (ga) ŋayi balaŋu rurrguyunara girri' nhanŋuwuy ŋayi. (You should have given (it to her) so that she could have washed the clothes.) MÄRR (GA)/BECAUSE: 1. Dhiyala limurru yurru nhina märr (ga) mulka'ŋura. (We'll sit here because (it's) dry.) NOTE: suffix -ŋura (mulka'ŋura) — the meaning seems to be 'because (we must sit) in a dry (spot)'; 2. Ŋayi dhu ŋäthili ḻuka märr (ga) ŋar'ŋaryunawuy yäna. (He must have a drink first because (he is) thirsty.); 3. Ŋarra yurru marrtji Bäḻmalili märr (ga) weṯimirrilili. (I'm going to Bäḻma because there are wallabies there.) NOTE: the adjective weṯimirri 'having wallabies' describes Bäḻma and takes the same -lili — 'because I want to go to a wallaby-inhabited place'. NOTES: 1. the bracketed (ga) may be omitted; it is not used at all at Yirrkala; 2. often märr (ga) becomes marr (ga) in pronunciation.

rules.statement: The phrase (ga) yäna bili ga translates 'until'; the bracketed (ga) is sometimes omitted: 1. Ŋarra ga nhina yäna barpuru (ga) yäna bili ga baḏayala bulŋuyukthirri. (Yesterday (last night) I just sat until the lights went out.); 2. Ŋarra gana ŋorrana yäna (ga) yäna bili ga djaḏaw'yurruna. (I slept until day broke.); 3. Nhe dhu ga djäma yäna (ga) yäna bili ga bell dhu wutthun. (You must work until the bell rings.); 4. Ŋayi dhu marrtji yäna (ga) yäna bili ga Darwin ŋayathama. (He'll walk until he reaches Darwin.); 5. Napurru marrtji traindhu (ga) yäna bili ga Alice Springs buna. (We went in the train until we came to Alice Springs (or as far as Alice Springs).) NOTES: 1. yäna (e.g. Ŋayi dhu marrtji yäna) has no real English equivalent — sometimes 'just'; 2. sometimes the second ga is omitted instead of the first, but never both at once.

examples.gup: Ŋayi dhu marrtji yäna bili ga ŋayi ga marrtji räli Darwinlili
examples.en: He'll go until he comes to Darwin

notes: The 'until'/'hasta que' branch joins with ' yäna bili ga ' (the ' ga yäna bili ' first-ga variant as alternativa per note 2); the dependent side reuses componerTemporal: 'he'll go until he comes to darwin' → Ŋayi dhu marrtji yäna bili ga ŋayi ga marrtji räli Darwinlili (the book's dep drops the pronoun and uses ŋayathama 'reaches' — attested)

Attested/pending: baḏayala bulŋuyukthirri 'lights go out' (ex 1), djaḏaw'yun 'day breaks' as a verb (ex 2 — the adverb djaḏaw'yunaray exists from L81), 'bell' (ex 3, also L95), Darwin ŋayathama bare-object reach (ex 4), traindhu instrumental 'in the train' + Alice Springs (ex 5), the yäna...yäna doubling in the mains

lessons.title: Dependent clauses (8) introduced by yurruna (before, then)

rules.statement: A. A yurruna clause BEFORE the main clause translates 'before': 1. Yurruna dhu nhe ŋorranydja, ŋathili djurra' ŋarraku wukirri. (Before you lie down, just write a letter for me.); 2. (religious example omitted by request). NOTES: 1. ŋathili/just, ŋäthili/first; 2. sometimes a connecting word (e.g. ga) joins the main clause when it follows the dependent. B. A yurruna clause AFTER the main clause translates 'before' or 'then': 1. Wiriny'tjurru ŋäthilinydja, yurruna dhu nhe ŋämindja. (Scrape (it) first, before you paint (it) / and then you can paint (it).); 2. Ŋayipi dhu ŋäthilinydja ḻuka ga yurruna dhu walalanhanydja ŋayi gurrupan. (He'll eat first himself before he gives (any) to them / and then he'll give (some) to them.) NOTE: Gupapuyŋu uses the FUTURE tense where English uses present ('Before you WILL eat your food, you...').

examples.gup: Yurruna nhe dhu ŋorra djorra' wukirri ŋarraku!
examples.en: Before you lie down write a letter for me

examples.gup: Ŋäthili ŋayi dhu ḻuka yurruna ŋayi ga gurrupan walalaŋgala
examples.en: He'll eat first before he gives it to them

notes: The 'before'/'antes (de) que' branch: before-first scans the split point and renders 'Yurruna <dep> <main>' (+ ga-link alternativa, note 2); before-mid joins ' yurruna '; the FUTURE note is code — componerTemporal now ALSO tries inserting 'will' after a leading pronoun, so 'before you lie down...' → Yurruna nhe dhu ŋorra ... (the book's Yurruna dhu nhe order and the -nydja suffixes attest); 'first' = ŋäthili added to vocab as adverbio (it was junk-naming Firstnha!): 'he'll eat first before he gives it to them' → Ŋäthili ŋayi dhu ḻuka yurruna ŋayi ga gurrupan walalaŋgala (B2 content; book's Ŋayipi emphatic and walalanhanydja attest)
Religious example omitted by request: A2
Attested/pending: ŋathili 'just' vs ŋäthili 'first' pair (note 1), wiriny'tjun 'scrape' and ŋäma- 'paint' verbs (B1), the dependent -nydja suffixes

lessons.title: Dependent clauses (9) introduced by dhäŋuru/dhurrwaraŋuru ŋuliŋuru (after)

rules.statement: A dependent clause introduced by dhäŋuru ŋuliŋuru or dhurrwaraŋuru ŋuliŋuru translates 'after': 1. Dhurrwaraŋuru/Dhäŋuru ŋuliŋuru walala bunhamina ga walalanydja ŋarali'na manaŋina. (After they had had a fight, they stole some tobacco.); 2. ... walala marrtjina ga ŋayinydja ŋarranha ŋäŋ'thurruna rrupiyawana. (After they had gone, he asked me for money.); 3. ... ŋunhi djamarrkuḻiny'tja marrtjina ga ŋarranydja bäru nhäŋala. (After the children had gone I saw a crocodile.); 4. ... ŋayi guya ḻukana, bala ŋayi rirrikthurruna. (After he ate the fish, he was sick.) NOTES: 1. the order of words may be reversed: Ŋuliŋuru(yi) dhäŋuru...; 2. when the dependent clause comes first the main clause is usually attached by a connecting word such as ga or bala; 3. it is more common to use only ONE clause: a. Dhäŋuru bunhaminyaŋuru walala ŋarali'na manaŋina. (After fighting they stole tobacco.); b. Dhäŋuru guyaŋuru ḻukanhaŋuru ŋayi rirrikthurruna. (After eating fish he became sick.); c. Dhäŋuru ŋathaŋuru ŋarranydja dhu marrtji guwatjman ŋanya. (After the meal I'll go and see him.)

examples.gup: Dhäŋuru ŋuliŋuru ŋayi guya ḻukana ga ŋayi rirrikthurruna
examples.en: After he ate the fish he was sick

examples.gup: Dhäŋuru ŋathaŋuru ŋarra ŋanya dhu guwatjman
examples.en: After the meal I'll visit him

notes: The 'after'/'después de que' branch: after-first scans the split point, the dependent parses as PAST (componerPasada — 'had' rewritten to 'have' like the L91 yanapi machinery), rendered 'Dhäŋuru ŋuliŋuru <dep> ga <main>' with dhurrwaraŋuru, the reversed Ŋuliŋuru-dhäŋuru order (note 1) and the bala link (note 2 — the book's own ex 4!) as alternativas; after-mid joins ' dhäŋuru ŋuliŋuru '. The note-3 ONE-CLAUSE form composes for noun dependents: 'after the meal i'll visit him' → Dhäŋuru ŋathaŋuru ŋarra ŋanya dhu guwatjman (= note-3c content — guwatjman IS the book's 'go and see'; 'meal' added to the ŋatha vocab entry)

Attested/pending: bunhamina 'had a fight' reciprocal (ex 1 + note-3a gerund 'after fighting' → bunhaminyaŋuru), ŋarali'na/-na object suffixes, 'after the children had gone' (noun-subject perfect doesn't parse yet), note-3b's double-ablative Dhäŋuru guyaŋuru ḻukanhaŋuru (nominalized-verb ablative), the -nydja dressing

lessons.title: Two clauses instead of one

rules.statement: To avoid some earlier constructions it is possible, at times, to use TWO clauses instead: 1. Ŋarra djäl nhänharawa mitjiyaŋgu (L44) can also be: Ŋarra djäl ŋarra dhu mitjiyaŋ nhäma. (I want to see the ship — lit. I want I shall see the ship.); 2. Guŋga'yurru ŋarranha märr-ŋamathinyarawa wiripuwurruŋgu (L45/83) can also be: Guŋga'yurru ŋarranha märr ga ŋarra dhu märr-ŋamathirri wiripuwurruŋgu. (Help me to love others.); 3. Ŋäŋ'thurru ŋanya ŋathawa bathanarawa can also be: Ŋäŋ'thurru ŋanya ŋayi dhu ŋatha bathan. (Ask her to cook the food — lit. ...she will cook the food.); 4. Ŋayi guyaŋana ŋathawa manaŋinyarawa (L45) can also be: Ŋayi guyaŋana ŋayi dhu ŋatha manaŋirri. (He thought of stealing some food. He thought he'd steal some food.); 5. (religious example omitted by request); 6. Ŋarra ga Djawaryun dhärranharay weyindhu (66) can also be: Ŋarra ga djawaryun bili ŋarra gana weyin dhärrana. (I'm tired because I was standing for a long time.)

examples.gup: Ŋarra djawaryurruna bili ŋarra gana weyin dhärrana
examples.en: I'm tired because I was standing for a long time

notes: THE FINAL LESSON — a validation lesson: the purpose-nominalizations (L44/45/83) and their finite two-clause paraphrases BOTH exist in the engine — the nominalization is the engine's main ('i want to see the ship' → Ŋarra djäl mitjiyaŋgu nhänharawa family) and the paraphrase family arrives via the subordination layer; ex 6 composes through the L98 because-branch: 'i'm tired because i was standing for a long time' → Ŋarra djawaryurruna bili ŋarra gana weyin dhärrana, whose 'Ŋarra ga djawaryun bili ...' alternativa IS the book's printed form (the probe also forced two mechanism fixes: 'for a long time' was junk-naming Timewa — 'time' and 'first' added to NO_SON_NOMBRES so the weyin duracion adverb wins)
